title: Air resistance, water resistance and upthrust: what slows a thing down, and what holds it up

summary.text: A loaded lunch box sits on a table with a thread tied to it. The thread goes over the table edge to a hanging bag, and you add spoonfuls of rice to the bag one at a time. It takes several spoonfuls before the box starts to slide. Now float the same box in a bucket of water. This time one paper clip hanging from the thread is enough to pull it across. Four contact forces explain this: friction, air resistance, water resistance and upthrust. Friction can hold a thing still, and it grows with the weight. Air resistance and water resistance act only on a thing that is moving, and they grow with speed. Upthrust is the upward push of water or air, and it acts on a still thing too. Your child finds the smallest pull that moves a floating load. They race three shapes of dough through water, and test a hole in a parachute. They draw every force as an arrow, and say whether the forces are balanced.
summary.art: A plastic lunch box full of rice floating in a bucket, pulled by a thread that runs over the rim to one hanging paper clip, beside the same box on a table pulled by a hanging cup of rice.

intro.hook: A lunch box holds two katoris of raw rice. It floats in a bucket of water. Could one hanging paper clip pull it across the water? Say yes or no, and say why.
intro.text: Most people say no, because the box feels heavy in the hand. In the experiment Table or Tub you test it. You pull the same loaded box on a table and then on water. You pull the same loaded box on a table and then on water. Each time you count how many spoonfuls of rice, or how many paper clips, it takes to start the box moving. In this unit you find out why water lets a heavy thing start so easily. You also find out why water and air push back hard on anything fast. Then you use both ideas to design a parachute.
intro.art: A child looking at a rice-filled lunch box floating in a bucket, holding up one paper clip on a thread, with a question mark above the bucket.

outcomes: By the end I can name friction, air resistance, water resistance and upthrust, and say which way each one acts.
By the end I can explain why friction can hold a thing still, and air and water resistance cannot.
By the end I can say how speed, front area, shape and the fluid change air and water resistance.
By the end I can explain upthrust, and say why a thing floats, sinks or hangs in water.
By the end I can draw a force diagram with several forces, and say if they are balanced.
By the end I can run a fair test with repeats, and say when a difference is too small to trust.
By the end I can design, test and improve a parachute, and explain it with forces.
By the end I can say what scientists still cannot work out about moving air and water.

terms.meaning: A fluid is anything that flows. Liquids and gases are fluids. Water and air are the two fluids we meet most.
terms.example: Air flows round a moving cycle, and water flows round a swimming fish.
terms.art: A fish in water and a cyclist in air, each with thin flow lines bending round them.

terms.meaning: Air resistance is the force from air on a thing that moves through it. It acts against the movement.
terms.example: Hold an open umbrella in front of you and run. The push you feel on the umbrella is air resistance.
terms.art: A girl running with an open umbrella held in front of her, with an arrow pointing backward from the umbrella.

terms.meaning: Water resistance is the force from water on a thing that moves through it. It acts against the movement.
terms.example: Wade across the shallow end of a pool. Your legs feel water resistance at every step.
terms.art: A child wading through knee-deep water, with arrows pointing backward from both legs.

terms.meaning: Drag is one word for air resistance and water resistance. It is the force from any fluid against a thing moving through it.
terms.example: A racing cyclist bends low over the handlebar to make her drag smaller.
terms.art: A racing cyclist bent low, with a short arrow pointing backward from her shoulders.

terms.meaning: Upthrust is the upward push of a fluid on a thing that is in it. It acts on still things and on moving things. It is also called buoyancy.
terms.example: Push an empty steel tumbler, open end up, down into a bucket of water. The push against your hand is upthrust.
terms.art: A hand pushing an empty steel tumbler down into a bucket of water, with a thick arrow pointing up from the tumbler.

terms.meaning: To displace water is to push it out of the way and take its place. A thing in water displaces as much water as the part of it that is under the surface.
terms.example: Lower a full bottle into a full bucket. The water that spills over is the water the bottle displaced.
terms.art: A bottle being lowered into a brim-full bucket standing in a tray, with water spilling over the rim into the tray.

terms.meaning: Friction is the force between two solid surfaces that touch. It acts against sliding, or against the sliding that would happen without it.
terms.example: A lunch box on a table stays still when you pull it gently. Friction from the table pulls back just as hard.
terms.art: A lunch box on a table with a thread pulling it one way and a friction arrow along the table pointing the other way.

terms.meaning: Gravity is the pull of the Earth on every thing. The size of that pull on a thing is called its weight.
terms.example: Gravity pulls a parachute and its load down all the time, even while they fall slowly.
terms.art: A small parachute with a coin, with one arrow pointing down from the coin.

terms.meaning: The normal force is the push of a solid surface on a thing that rests on it. It points straight out of the surface.
terms.example: A table pushes up on a lunch box with a normal force. That push holds the box up.
terms.art: A lunch box on a table with an arrow pointing up from the table into the box.

terms.meaning: A force diagram is a simple drawing of one thing with an arrow for each force on it. A bigger force gets a longer arrow.
terms.example: A floating box gets two arrows of the same length. Gravity points down and upthrust points up.
terms.art: A box on a water line with one arrow down labelled gravity and one arrow up of the same length labelled upthrust.

terms.meaning: Forces on a thing are balanced when they cancel each other. Then the thing stays still, or keeps moving at the same speed in a straight line.
terms.example: A boat floating at a jetty has balanced forces. Gravity pulls down and upthrust pushes up just as hard.
terms.art: A boat at a jetty with an arrow up and an arrow down of equal length.

terms.meaning: Forces on a thing are unbalanced when one side is bigger. Then the thing speeds up, slows down or turns.
terms.example: A mango that has just left the branch speeds up. Gravity is far bigger than the air resistance on it.
terms.art: A falling mango with a long arrow down and a very short arrow up.

terms.meaning: Terminal speed is the steady speed a falling thing reaches when air or water resistance has grown to balance gravity. After that the thing falls no faster.
terms.example: A raindrop reaches its terminal speed after a few metres. It then falls at about 30 kilometres an hour, all the way down.
terms.art: A raindrop with an arrow down and an arrow up of equal length, and a level line on a small speed graph beside it.

terms.meaning: The front area of a moving thing is the area it pushes through the air or water. It is the size of the shape you see from straight ahead.
terms.example: A flat hand swept through water has a big front area. The same hand held edge-on has a small one.
terms.art: A hand seen from in front, first flat and wide, then edge-on and thin, with the two outlines shaded.

terms.meaning: A streamlined shape lets air or water flow round it and close up smoothly behind. It is rounded at the front and narrows slowly to the back.
terms.example: A rohu fish is streamlined. Her body is rounded at the head and narrows to the tail.
terms.art: A side view of a rohu fish with smooth flow lines passing round her body and joining again behind the tail.

terms.meaning: The wake is the stirred-up air or water that a moving thing leaves behind it. A big wake means the thing has given a lot of its energy to the fluid.
terms.example: A flat-backed lorry leaves a wide wake of swirling air. You feel it as a gust when a lorry passes you on the road.
terms.art: A flat-backed lorry on a road with large swirls of air drawn behind it.

terms.meaning: The canopy is the wide sheet of a parachute. It pushes a large front area through the air.
terms.example: A square of polythene 30 centimetres wide makes a canopy for a parachute that carries one coin.
terms.art: A small square polythene parachute with four threads and a coin, with the word canopy pointing at the sheet.

terms.meaning: A vent is a small hole in the top of a parachute canopy. It lets a little air out through the middle, so less air spills out at the edges.
terms.example: Almost every round parachute has a vent at the top.
terms.art: A round parachute seen from above with a small round hole in the centre, and small arrows of air rising through the hole.

explanations.concept: Four contact forces: friction, air resistance, water resistance and upthrust
explanations.definition: Friction acts between two solid surfaces that touch. Air resistance and water resistance act on a thing that moves through air or water. Upthrust is the upward push of water or air on a thing in it.
explanations.description: All four are contact forces. They act only where a thing touches a surface, the air or the water. Gravity is different, because it acts across a gap. Each of the four has its own direction. Friction lies along the surfaces and acts against sliding. Air resistance and water resistance point against the movement through the air or water. Upthrust always points up, whichever way the thing moves. A boat on a lake has three of them at once. Upthrust holds the boat up, and water resistance and air resistance slow the boat down.
examples: A girl cycling on a flat road has friction at her tyres and air resistance on her body.
A swimmer gliding after a push from the wall has upthrust holding her up and water resistance slowing her.
A stone lying on the bottom of a pond has upthrust on it too. The upthrust is smaller than the stone's weight.
explanations.art: A lake scene with a rowing boat, a cyclist on the bank and a stone on the lake bed, each with labelled force arrows.

explanations.concept: Friction can hold a thing still. Air and water resistance cannot
explanations.definition: Friction between solids can match a pull and hold a thing still. Air resistance and water resistance are zero on a thing that is not moving through the air or water.
explanations.description: Pull gently on a loaded box on a table, and the box stays where it is. Friction from the table pulls back exactly as hard as you pull. It can do so up to a limit, and that limit grows with the weight of the box. A heavier box needs a bigger pull to start. Water resistance works in another way. It comes from pushing water out of the way, so a thing at rest has none. Even the smallest pull is unbalanced, and the floating thing starts to move. It starts slowly if it has a lot of mass, because mass makes a thing slow to change its speed. So nothing that floats can be held in place by the water alone. Boats are tied to a jetty or held by an anchor in the sea bed.
examples: In Table or Tub, a loaded lunch box on the table needed several spoons of rice to start it. Afloat, one paper clip started it.
Two people with a rope can pull a floating houseboat to the bank at Alappuzha. They could never drag the same boat up the bank.
Long ago, one horse on a canal path pulled a boat carrying tens of tonnes. On a road the same horse pulled a cart of one or two tonnes.
explanations.art: Two drawings side by side: a loaded box on a table held still by a friction arrow, and the same box afloat with one small pull arrow and no arrow against it.

explanations.concept: What makes air resistance and water resistance bigger
explanations.definition: Drag grows with speed, with front area and with a blunt shape. It is far bigger in water than in air at the same speed.
explanations.description: Four things decide the size of drag. The first is speed. At twice the speed, a thing meets about four times the drag. The second is front area. A wide front has to push more air or water out of the way each second. The third is shape. A flat plate has many times the drag of a streamlined shape with the same front area. The fourth is the fluid. One litre of water has about 800 times the mass of one litre of air. So water pushes back far harder than air at the same speed. Weight is not on this list. A heavy thing and a light thing of the same size, shape and speed meet the same drag.
examples: In Newspaper on Your Chest, a full sheet stayed up at a walk. Folded in half, the same sheet needed a faster walk.
In the Sinking Race, a flat pancake of dough sank far more slowly than a ball of equal dough.
Most of the effort of a fast cyclist goes into pushing air out of the way.
You can run in air. In chest-deep water you can only wade.
explanations.art: Four small pictures in a row: a slow and a fast cyclist, a flat hand and an edge-on hand in water, a flat plate and a fish shape, and a runner in air beside a wader in water.

explanations.concept: Streamlined shapes: a rounded front and a long, narrowing back
explanations.definition: A streamlined shape is rounded at the front and narrows slowly towards the back. Air or water flows round it and closes up smoothly behind it.
explanations.description: Many people think a streamlined shape needs a sharp point at the front. The back matters more. Behind a blunt back, the air or water cannot close up smoothly. It breaks into swirls, and this swirling region is the wake. The moving thing has to keep giving energy to those swirls. A long, narrowing back lets the fluid close up gently, so the wake is small. That is why a fish, a dolphin and an aeroplane body are all rounded in front and narrow behind. A falling raindrop is not pointed at the top. A small drop is round, and a big drop is flat underneath, like a bun.
examples: In the Sinking Race, a carrot shape dropped thick end first sank faster than a ball of the same dough.
A racing cycle helmet is rounded in front and has a long tail behind the head.
Lorries with a flat back leave a wide wake. Some carry sloping panels at the back to make the wake smaller.
The Ganges river dolphin and the rohu are far apart on the tree of life. Their bodies have nearly the same outline.
explanations.art: A flat plate, a ball and a fish shape in flowing water, with a large swirling wake behind the plate, a medium one behind the ball and almost none behind the fish shape.

explanations.concept: Upthrust: the push that equals the weight of the water displaced
explanations.definition: The upthrust on a thing equals the weight of the water or air that the thing displaces. This is Archimedes' principle.
explanations.description: A thing under water takes up space where water used to be. Before the thing came, the water around that space held the missing water up. That surrounding water has not changed. So it pushes up on the new thing just as hard as it pushed on that water. This means upthrust depends on the size of the part under water. It does not depend on what the thing is made of, or on how heavy it is. A full bottle, an empty bottle and a bottle of coins of the same size get the same upthrust. Upthrust acts on sinking things too. A stone feels lighter under water because the upthrust carries part of its weight.
examples: In Three Bottles, all three bottles raised the water in the bucket by the same amount. So all three got the same upthrust.
In the Bag of Water, a bag of water hung from a rubber band. In the bucket the band went slack, because the upthrust equalled the weight of the bag.
A floating box with two katoris of rice sits deeper than with one. It must displace more water to get more upthrust.
explanations.art: A bucket of water with a dotted outline of a bottle-shaped space, small arrows from the surrounding water pushing up on it, and the same arrows pushing up on a real bottle beside it.

explanations.concept: Why water pushes up: deeper water presses harder
explanations.definition: Water presses on every surface it touches, and it presses harder the deeper you go. The underside of a thing is deeper than its top, so the push up is bigger than the push down.
explanations.description: Water is made of tiny particles that are always moving and bumping into whatever they touch. Deep water has more water resting on it, so its particles are squeezed together harder. They press harder on everything, in every direction. Think of a tumbler held under water. The water under it pushes up. The water over it pushes down. The water under it is deeper, so the upward push wins. The difference between the two pushes is the upthrust. Once the tumbler is fully under, pushing it deeper does not change the upthrust. Both pushes grow by the same amount, so the difference stays the same.
examples: In Three Bottles, you held the empty bottle near the surface and near the bottom. It pushed up on your hand equally hard in both places.
A diver's ears hurt in the deep end of a pool, because the deeper water presses harder on the eardrums.
Air does the same thing. It presses a little harder at your feet than at your head, so air gives you a very small upthrust.
explanations.art: A tumbler under water with small arrows pressing on its top and longer arrows pressing on its underside, and a depth scale at the side.

explanations.concept: Float, sink or hang: upthrust against gravity
explanations.definition: A thing fully under water rises if its upthrust is bigger than its weight. It sinks if its weight is bigger. It hangs in place if the two are equal.
explanations.description: Compare a thing with the water it displaces. If the thing weighs less than that water, the upthrust is bigger than gravity and the thing rises. At the surface part of the thing comes out. Now the thing displaces less water, and the upthrust shrinks until it equals the weight. That is floating. If the thing weighs more than the water it displaces, it sinks. If the two weights are equal, the thing hangs wherever you leave it. A steel ship floats because its hollow hull displaces a huge amount of water. The air inside does not lift the ship. The air only keeps the ship light for its size.
examples: A bottle full of water hangs or sinks very slowly in a bucket. It weighs almost exactly as much as the water it displaces.
A rohu changes the amount of gas in her swim bladder until she hangs in the water without swimming.
A submarine takes water into its tanks to sink, and pushes the water out with air to rise.
Most sharks have no swim bladder. Many of them sink slowly if they stop swimming.
explanations.art: Three bottles in a tank: one bobbing at the surface, one hanging in the middle and one on the bottom, each with a gravity arrow and an upthrust arrow of different lengths.

explanations.definition: When the forces on a thing are balanced, its speed does not change. A still thing stays still, and a moving thing keeps the same speed.
explanations.description: People often think a moving thing must have a force pushing it along. It does not. Forces are needed to change a speed, not to keep one. A coin dropped in water speeds up at first, because gravity is bigger than the upthrust. As the coin gets faster, the water resistance grows. Soon the upthrust and the water resistance together equal gravity. From then on the forces are balanced, and the coin sinks at a steady speed. This steady speed is called the terminal speed. Here is the surprising part. At terminal speed, the resistance equals the weight minus the upthrust, whatever the shape. A wide shape reaches that much resistance at a low speed. A streamlined shape has to go much faster to reach it.
examples: In the Sinking Race, the pancake and the carrot were equal pieces of dough. Once each sank steadily, the water resistance on both was the same. The pancake met it at a low speed.
A skydiver lying flat falls at about 200 kilometres an hour and gets no faster.
A raindrop falls from a cloud two kilometres up. Without air it would land at about 700 kilometres an hour. With air it lands at about 30.
explanations.art: A sinking coin drawn three times down the page, with the upward arrows growing from short to equal with the downward arrow, and a speed graph that rises and then runs level.

explanations.concept: How a parachute works, and why it has a hole
explanations.definition: A parachute gives a falling load a very large front area. The air resistance then balances gravity at a low speed, so the load lands gently.
explanations.description: Gravity pulls a load down just as hard with a parachute as without one. The canopy changes the speed at which air resistance grows big enough to balance that pull. A big canopy reaches the balance at a low speed. A heavier load under the same canopy must fall faster before the forces balance. So the size of the canopy is chosen to suit the load. Air caught under a canopy has to get out. If it can only spill out at the edges, it spills from one side and then the other. That makes the parachute swing. A small vent at the top lets some air out through the middle. The parachute swings less, and the fall is hardly any faster. The strings matter too. Short strings pull the canopy into a narrow cup with a smaller front area.
examples: In A Hole in the Parachute, you cut a small vent in a polythene canopy. Then you compared the fall time and the landing place.
A skydiver slows from about 200 kilometres an hour to about 20 when her canopy opens.
The crew capsule of ISRO's Gaganyaan is designed to come down to the sea under large parachutes.
The fluff round a silk cotton seed works as a parachute made of fine hairs with gaps between them.
explanations.art: A round parachute falling straight with a small vent at the top and air rising through it, beside a parachute with no vent tilting to one side as air spills from under one edge.

explanations.concept: Where the movement goes: resistance warms the air and the water
explanations.definition: Air resistance and water resistance take kinetic energy from a moving thing. The energy goes into moving the fluid, and it ends as heat.
explanations.description: Energy is never destroyed. A boat that slows down has passed its kinetic energy to the water. First the water moves as waves and swirls in the wake. Then the swirls die away, and the water is left very slightly warmer. The same happens in air. At everyday speeds the warming is far too small to feel. At very high speeds it is enormous. A space capsule meets the air at about 28,000 kilometres an hour. It squashes the air in front of it so hard that the air glows white hot. Most of that heat comes from the squashing of the air, and only a little from rubbing. A thick heat shield protects the crew.
examples: Stir a bucket of water hard and take the spoon out. The swirls slow down and stop, and their energy is now heat in the water.
A meteor glows because the air squashed in front of it becomes white hot.
A parachute falling at a steady speed is warming the air a little all the way down.
explanations.art: A space capsule coming down with a glowing layer of squashed air in front of its heat shield, and a small inset of a spoon stirring a bucket with swirls fading away.

explanations.concept: Is air resistance a kind of friction?
explanations.definition: Some books call air resistance and water resistance kinds of friction. Many scientists keep them apart from friction.
explanations.description: The three forces are alike in some ways. All are contact forces, all act against a movement, and all turn kinetic energy into heat. They also differ. Friction between solids can hold a thing still, and it changes little with speed. Drag is zero on a still thing and grows fast with speed. Friction grows with weight, and drag does not. The causes differ too. Solid friction comes from two surfaces gripping each other at many tiny spots. Most drag comes from having to push fluid out of the way. A smaller part comes from fluid rubbing along the sides, and that part is truly like friction. So the name depends on which likeness you think matters most.
examples: In Table or Tub, friction held the box still against a pull. Water resistance could not.
A long, thin racing boat has little water to push aside. Most of its drag is water rubbing along its sides.
A flat plate pulled face-on through water has almost no rubbing along its sides. Nearly all its drag comes from pushing water aside.

perspectives.explanation: They call air resistance and water resistance kinds of friction. All three act against movement where things touch, and all three make heat.
They use the word drag and keep it apart from friction. Drag is zero at rest, grows with speed and comes mostly from pushing fluid aside.

explanations.art: Two columns headed friction and drag, with small pictures: a box held still on a slope under friction, and a still boat with no arrow and a fast boat with a long arrow under drag.

explanations.concept: Why nobody can work out exactly how water and air swirl
explanations.definition: Swirling, tumbling flow is called turbulence. Scientists have equations for moving fluids, but nobody can solve them exactly for turbulent flow.
explanations.description: Slow flow round a smooth shape is orderly. Faster flow breaks into swirls of many sizes, and big swirls break into smaller ones. This is turbulence, and most of the drag on cars, ships and aeroplanes comes with it. The equations for a moving fluid were written down about two hundred years ago. They are named after Claude-Louis Navier and George Stokes. For turbulent flow, nobody has been able to solve them exactly. Engineers get useful answers in two ways. They test models in wind tunnels and in long tanks of water. They also use large computers that work out the flow in millions of small steps. Both ways give good estimates, and both still get surprises.
examples: Smoke from an incense stick rises in a smooth line and then suddenly breaks into swirls. That change is the start of turbulence.
Ship designers still pull model hulls along a tank of water before a ship is built.
A prize of one million dollars was offered in the year 2000 for a full mathematical answer. In 2026 a claimed answer is being looked at.

perspectives.explanation: Models and computer estimates are good enough to design safe ships and aeroplanes. An exact answer is not needed for that.
Without an exact answer we cannot be sure the equations always work. So the question stayed open for a long time. A claimed answer is now being checked.

explanations.art: A stick of incense with smoke rising in a straight line for a hand's width and then breaking into curling swirls.

agreed.text: Friction, air resistance, water resistance and upthrust are contact forces. Each acts only where a thing touches a surface, the air or the water.
agreed.evidence: In 1971 a feather and a hammer were dropped on the Moon. They landed together, because the Moon has no air to touch them.

agreed.text: Air resistance and water resistance are zero on a thing at rest, and grow quickly with speed. At twice the speed they are about four times as big.
agreed.evidence: Engineers measure the force on cars in wind tunnels, at many speeds. They do the same for model ships pulled along tanks of water.

agreed.text: The upthrust on a thing equals the weight of the water or air it displaces.
agreed.evidence: Archimedes wrote this down about 2,250 years ago. Every ship's load line and every submarine dive depends on it.

agreed.text: When the forces on a thing are balanced, the thing keeps the speed it has.
agreed.evidence: Skydivers stop speeding up at about 200 kilometres an hour, when air resistance has grown to equal their weight.

agreed.text: A streamlined shape can have under one tenth of the drag of a flat plate with the same front area.
agreed.evidence: Wind tunnel and water tank tests of plates, balls and fish-like shapes have shown this for over a hundred years.

agreed.text: The energy that air and water resistance take from a moving thing ends as heat in the air or water.
agreed.evidence: The air in front of a returning space capsule glows white hot. The capsule slows from orbit speed to parachute speed.

challenging.claim: A streamlined shape needs a sharp point at the front.
challenging.who: Many people, and many drawings of rockets and fast cars
challenging.for: At speeds faster than sound, a sharp nose does help. Pointed bows also help ships cut through waves.
challenging.against: At everyday speeds the back matters more than the front. A rounded front and a long, narrowing back give the smallest wake. Fish, dolphins and aeroplane bodies are all rounded in front.
challenging.context: This card is about a common belief: that a pointed front is what makes a shape streamlined.

challenging.claim: A parachute works because it makes the air resistance bigger than the weight.
challenging.for: For a few seconds after the canopy opens, air resistance really is bigger than the weight. That is why the fall slows down.
challenging.against: Once the fall is steady, air resistance exactly equals the weight. If it stayed bigger, the parachute would slow to a stop and then rise. The canopy lowers the speed at which the two forces balance.
challenging.context: This card is about what a parachute really changes: the size of the air resistance, or the speed at which it balances gravity.

challenging.claim: Air resistance and water resistance are kinds of friction.
challenging.for: All three are contact forces, act against movement and make heat. Part of drag is fluid rubbing along a surface.
challenging.against: Friction can hold a thing still and grows with weight. Drag is zero at rest, grows with speed and does not depend on weight. Most drag comes from pushing fluid aside.
challenging.context: This card is about a naming question. Should air and water resistance be called friction?

challenging.claim: Upthrust acts only on things that float.
challenging.for: We notice upthrust most when it wins. A ball pushed under water jumps back up.
challenging.against: A stone feels lighter under water than in air. The water pushes up on the stone too. The push is only smaller than the stone's weight.
challenging.context: This card is about a common belief: that the water pushes up only on floating things.

challenging.claim: A space capsule gets hot because it rubs against the air.
challenging.for: Air does rub along the sides of the capsule, and that makes some heat.
challenging.against: Most of the heat comes from the air in front being squashed very hard and very fast. Squashed air gets hot, as a cycle pump does when you pump quickly.
challenging.context: This card is about why things get hot when they come back from space.

challenging.claim: Heavy things always fall faster than light things.
challenging.who: Aristotle, and most people before they test it
challenging.for: In air it is often true. Two things of the same size and shape meet the same air resistance. The heavier one needs a higher speed before that resistance balances its weight.
challenging.against: Where there is no air, everything falls together. In air, a wide light thing and a narrow heavy thing can fall in either order. Shape and size matter as much as weight.
challenging.context: This card is about a very old belief: that heavier things fall faster.

big_questions.q: A boat that is standing still feels no water resistance, but a moving boat does. So does the resistance come from the water, or from the movement?
big_questions.hint: Think about a boat drifting along with a river. Is she moving or still, for the water around her?

big_questions.q: A bag of water hung in a bucket of water feels weightless, because the upthrust holds it up. So does the water in the middle of a lake have any weight?
big_questions.hint: Ask what is holding that water up, and what it is holding up in turn.

big_questions.q: Fish, dolphins and penguins are not close relatives, yet they have nearly the same shape. Who chose that shape?
big_questions.hint: Think about which animals caught more food and escaped more hunters, over millions of years in the same water.

big_questions.q: Going twice as fast means about four times the drag. Is it worth the fuel to save an hour?
big_questions.hint: Think of a ferry, a train and a plane. Who gains the hour, and who pays for the fuel and the smoke?

big_questions.q: You live at the bottom of an ocean of air, and its upthrust goes unnoticed. What else pushes on you without your noticing?
big_questions.hint: Think of things that have always been there, so you have nothing to compare them with.

big_questions.q: If nothing ever resisted movement, would a moving thing ever stop?
big_questions.hint: Think of a spacecraft far from any planet, with its engine switched off.

story.title: The Garden on a Rope
story.note: A made-up story. Zooni, Dadi, Ammi and Bilal are imagined. These things are real. Growers on Dal Lake in Srinagar raise vegetables on floating gardens made of matted lake reeds and mud. The gardens are held in place by poles pushed into the lake bed. A garden can be untied and towed to a new place. Growers sell vegetables from boat to boat at a floating market at dawn. The size and weight of the garden in the story are guesses.
text: The wind came down from the mountains in the night. It shook the shutters and rattled the tin roof of the kitchen. In the morning Dal Lake lay flat and grey, as if nothing had happened.

Zooni was ten. She stepped out onto the wet planks of the landing and counted the family's floating gardens, as she did every morning. One, two, three. She counted again. The fourth garden, the one with the tomatoes, was gone.

'Dadi!' she shouted. Her grandmother came out slowly, one hand on her knee. Dadi looked across the water and pointed with her chin. Far down the channel, against the lotus beds, lay a long green strip with red dots on it.

A floating garden is not a small thing. This one was as long as three boats laid end to end, and as wide as a bed. It was made of lake reeds, piled and pressed and rotted together for years, with black mud on top. Tomatoes grew on it as if it were land. Two willow poles, pushed down through it into the lake bed, had held it in its place. In the night both poles had snapped.

'Ammi has the big boat,' said Zooni. Her mother had left before dawn for the vegetable market, where the growers sell from boat to boat. 'She will not be back till noon. By then the wind may take the garden right out into the lake.'
'Then you will bring it home,' said Dadi.

Zooni stared at her. 'Me? Dadi, it is heavier than a lorry. Last winter it took six men to drag our small boat up the bank. Six men, for a boat that I can lift at one end! How many men would that garden need?'
'On the bank, a great many,' said Dadi. 'Take the small boat and the long rope. Go.'

Zooni paddled down the channel with the rope coiled at her feet. Her cousin Bilal was mending a net on the next landing. 'You will never move that,' he called. 'You need a motor!' She did not answer. She thought he was right.

She tied the rope round the stump of a broken pole at the corner of the garden. Then she turned the boat towards home and paddled as hard as she could. The rope sprang up out of the water, dripping, and went tight. The boat stopped as if it had hit a wall. Zooni dug the paddle in again and again. Water foamed behind her. Her arms burned. The tomato plants did not even shake.
'It is stuck!' she shouted across the water. 'I told you!'
Dadi's voice came back thin and clear. 'Stop splashing. Keep the rope tight. Pull gently, and count to a hundred.'

Zooni was too tired to argue. She paddled with small, slow strokes, only enough to keep the rope out of the water. One, two, three. Nothing. Twenty. Nothing. At thirty she looked at the lotus leaves beside the garden, to rest her eyes. A leaf that had been touching the reeds was now a hand's width away from them.
She kept counting. At fifty the gap was as wide as her boat. At eighty the whole long garden was sliding after her down the channel, tomatoes and all, without a sound.
Bilal had put down his net. 'How are you doing that?' he called.

'I don't know!' said Zooni. She was so pleased that she began to paddle fast, to bring the garden home sooner. At once the paddle grew heavy, and the rope pulled hard at the boat. She paddled faster still. Her arms burned again, and the garden came along hardly any quicker than before.
She let her strokes go slow. The pull went soft again. The garden kept coming.
So that was how it was. The water had not pushed back because the garden was heavy. It pushed back when she hurried.

The home poles were still six boat-lengths away when Dadi called again. 'Now stop pulling.' Zooni lifted her paddle, and the rope went slack. The garden did not stop. It came on, slow and wide, and nothing in the water could hold it. It slid on and on, a little slower with every boat-length. At last it touched the cucumber garden with a small bump and lay still.

Dadi was waiting with two new willow poles. Together they pushed them down through the reeds, through the water, and into the mud of the lake bed. Zooni leaned on her pole until it would go no deeper.
'Dadi,' she said. 'Six men for the small boat on the bank. One girl for the garden on the water. Why?'

'On the bank, the ground holds on to a thing,' said Dadi. 'The heavier the thing, the harder the ground holds. On the lake, the water carries the weight, and it holds on to nothing. A sparrow could move this garden, if she pulled for long enough.'
'Then why do we need the poles?'
'Because the water holds on to nothing,' said Dadi. 'And the wind pulls for a long time.'

At noon Ammi's boat came round the bend with its empty baskets. She looked at the four gardens, and at the two pale new poles. 'They told me at the market that our tomatoes had gone to the lotus beds,' she said. 'Who brought them back?'
'I did,' said Zooni. 'Slowly.'

That evening she lay on the planks and put one finger against the edge of the tomato garden. She pushed gently, and kept pushing. Very slowly the whole long garden leaned away from her, until the new poles creaked and held.
story.epiphany: For the parent: on land, friction holds a heavy thing still, and it grows with the weight. That is why six men were needed for a small boat on the bank. Afloat, upthrust carries the weight, and water resistance is zero on a thing that is not moving. So even a small, steady pull moves a very heavy garden. It starts slowly, because a large mass takes a long time to speed up. Water resistance grows with speed, so hurrying costs far more effort for little gain. And because water cannot hold anything in place, a floating garden needs poles in the lake bed.
ask: Six men were needed to drag a small boat up a bank. One girl moved a huge garden on the water. What was different?
Why did hard paddling at the start seem to do nothing, while gentle pulling for a long count worked?
When Zooni paddled fast, the pull on the rope grew much harder. Which force grew, and why?
The garden kept moving after Zooni stopped pulling. Which force slowed it in the end?
Why can poles in the lake bed hold the garden in place when the water cannot?

games.title: Which Forces? A card game of balanced and unbalanced forces
games.context: This is a card game about the forces on one thing. Each card describes a thing that floats, sinks, falls, slides or rests. You lay down a token for every force on it, and say whether the forces are balanced.

printables.title: 20 situation cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: A loaded rice boat floats still beside a jetty. Which forces act on the boat?
items.b: Two forces act on the boat: gravity and upthrust. They are balanced. The boat is still, so there is no water resistance.

items.f: A stone lies still on the bottom of a pond. Which forces act on the stone?
items.b: Three forces act on the stone: gravity, upthrust and the normal force from the pond floor. They are balanced. Upthrust acts on sunk things too.

items.f: A skydiver falls at a steady speed under her open parachute. Which forces act on her?
items.b: Two forces act on her: gravity and air resistance. They are balanced. At a steady speed, air resistance equals her weight.

items.f: A mango has just left the branch and is starting to fall. Which forces act on the mango?
items.b: Only gravity acts on the mango. The forces are unbalanced. The mango is still slow, so air resistance is almost nothing yet.

items.f: A girl cycles along a flat road at a steady speed. Which forces act on her and her cycle?
items.b: Four forces act: gravity, the normal force, friction and air resistance. They are balanced. Friction at the back tyre pushes her forward, and air resistance pushes back.

items.f: A book lies still on a flat table. Which forces act on the book?
items.b: Two forces act on the book: gravity and the normal force. They are balanced. Nothing is trying to slide the book, so there is no friction.

items.f: A swimmer glides forward under water after pushing off the wall. Which forces act on her?
items.b: Three forces act on her: gravity, upthrust and water resistance. They are unbalanced. Nothing pushes her forward now, so water resistance slows her.

items.f: A rohu fish hangs still in the middle of a pond. Which forces act on her?
items.b: Two forces act on her: gravity and upthrust. They are balanced. She has set her swim bladder so that upthrust equals her weight.

items.f: A coin sinks through deep water at a steady speed. Which forces act on the coin?
items.b: Three forces act on the coin: gravity, upthrust and water resistance. They are balanced. The two upward forces together equal gravity.

items.f: A carrom coin slides across the board and slows down. Which forces act on the coin?
items.b: Three forces act on the coin: gravity, the normal force and friction. They are unbalanced. Friction acts against the slide, and nothing pushes the coin on.

items.f: A balloon filled with helium has just been let go and is speeding up. Which forces act on it?
items.b: Two forces act on the balloon: gravity and upthrust from the air. They are unbalanced. The upthrust is bigger than the balloon's weight.

items.f: A tugboat pushes a ship sideways at a slow, steady speed. Which forces act on the ship?
items.b: Four forces act on the ship: gravity, upthrust, the tugboat's push and water resistance. They are balanced. The push equals the water resistance.

items.f: A child slides down a playground slide at a steady speed. Which forces act on the child?
items.b: Three forces act on the child: gravity, the normal force and friction. They are balanced. The three forces cancel, so the speed stays the same.

items.f: A hand holds a ball still under water. Which forces act on the ball?
items.b: Three forces act on the ball: gravity, upthrust and a push from the hand. They are balanced. The hand pushes down, because the upthrust is bigger than the ball's weight.

items.f: A hand has just let go of a ball under water. Which forces act on the ball?
items.b: Two forces act on the ball: gravity and upthrust. They are unbalanced. The upthrust is bigger, so the ball speeds upward.

items.f: A box is pushed across a floor at a steady speed. Which forces act on the box?
items.b: Four forces act on the box: gravity, the normal force, a push and friction. They are balanced. The push equals the friction.

items.f: A space capsule is falling very fast when its parachute opens. Which forces act on the capsule?
items.b: Two forces act on the capsule: gravity and air resistance. They are unbalanced. For a few seconds air resistance is bigger than gravity, so the capsule slows down.

items.f: An astronaut drops a hammer on the Moon. Which forces act on the falling hammer?
items.b: Only gravity acts on the hammer. The forces are unbalanced. The Moon has no air, so nothing acts against the fall.

items.f: A loaded box floats still in a tub. A thread has just begun to pull it. Which forces act on the box?
items.b: Three forces act on the box: gravity, upthrust and the pull. They are unbalanced. The box is still at rest, so there is no water resistance yet.

items.f: A lorry is parked on a sloping road. Which forces act on the lorry?
items.b: Three forces act on the lorry: gravity, the normal force and friction. They are balanced. Friction up the slope stops the lorry sliding down.

printables.title: 7 force tokens for each player to copy and cut out

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, question side up. Each player lays out their seven force tokens.
One player reads the top card aloud.
Each player pushes forward a token for every force on the thing. Count only the main forces, and leave out any that are too small to matter.
Turn the card over. A player with exactly the right tokens scores 1 point. A right call of balanced or unbalanced scores 1 more.
After 20 cards, the player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: score in the same way. Try to reach 30 points out of 40, then play again.

setup.art: A pile of question cards on a table and a row of seven small paper tokens with force names in front of each of two players.
setup.caption: 1. Put the cards in a pile. Each player lays out seven force tokens.

setup.art: A child pushing forward three tokens labelled gravity, upthrust and water resistance while another child reads a card.
setup.caption: 2. Read the card. Push forward a token for every force on the thing.

setup.art: The card turned over to show its answer, with two players comparing their tokens with it.
setup.caption: 3. Say 'balanced' or 'unbalanced'. Then turn the card to check.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 20 cards. 2. Each player copies the seven force names onto slips of paper. 3. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, question side up.
flow.say: Each card describes one thing. We will find every force on that thing, and then say whether the forces are balanced.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Write the seven force names on slips of paper. Shuffle the cards.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Forces. Here you set up the cards and the force tokens.

flow.do: 1. Read the top card aloud. 2. Everyone pushes forward their tokens. 3. Everyone says 'balanced' or 'unbalanced'. 4. Turn the card over and read the reason.
flow.say: Ask two questions for every card. What is this thing touching? Is its speed changing? The first gives the forces, and the second tells you about balance.
flow.kid: Read the card. What does the thing touch? Is its speed changing? Push your tokens forward.

ask.q: A stone lies on the bottom of a pond. Why does it get an upthrust token?
good: The stone displaces water, so the water pushes up on it.
Upthrust acts on everything in water, and here it is smaller than the weight.

flow.parent: The speed gives the balance. A thing that is still or moving steadily has balanced forces. A thing that is speeding up or slowing down has unbalanced forces.
flow.context: This is the main part of Which Forces. Here you read each card, choose the forces and say whether they are balanced.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Lay out the cards that anyone got wrong. 3. Sort all 20 cards into two heaps: balanced and unbalanced. 4. Ask what every card in the balanced heap has in common.
flow.say: Look at the balanced heap. Some of those things are still, and some are moving. What is the same about all of them?
flow.kid: Count your points. Sort the cards into balanced and unbalanced. What is the same in the balanced heap?

check.q: A coin sinks through deep water at a steady speed. Which forces act on the coin?
check.why: Gravity pulls the coin down. The water pushes up on it with upthrust, and water resistance acts against its movement. Leaving out upthrust usually means thinking that upthrust acts only on floating things.

flow.context: This is the last step of Which Forces. Here you count the points and sort the cards.

games.title: Open It in Time: a bean game about falling
games.context: This is a counting game about a skydiver. The beans in your hand are your speed. Gravity gives you beans every turn, and the air takes some back. You choose when to open your parachute, and you must land slowly enough to be safe.

printables.title: The height track, drawn on two sheets of paper
items: Draw 60 squares in a long winding line.
Number the squares from 60 at the top down to 1.

printables.title: 4 jumpers, one for each player (buttons or coins also work)
Score sheet for one jump
items: Turn number | Beans after gravity | Beans given back to the air | Beans left, which is my speed | My square
I opened my parachute at the start of turn: __
Turns I took to reach the ground: __
Beans in my hand when I landed: __
Safe landing, with 4 beans or fewer? __

rules: Each player needs about 15 beans, seeds or small coins. Put your jumper on square 60 and start with no beans. The beans in your hand are your speed.
Every turn has three parts. First, gravity: take 3 beans.
Second, air resistance. With your parachute closed, give back 1 bean for every 4 you hold. With it open, give back 1 bean for every 2 you hold. Leftover beans stay with you.
Third, fall: move your jumper down one square for each bean you still hold.
At the start of any turn you may say 'Open!'. Your parachute then stays open for the rest of the jump.
You land safely if you hold 4 beans or fewer when you reach the ground. With more than 4 you have crashed.
Among the players who land safely, the one who took the fewest turns wins.
Playing alone: find the latest turn on which you can open your parachute and still land safely.
Harder game: a heavy jumper takes 4 beans from gravity every turn, and may land with 5 beans or fewer.

setup.art: A winding track of 60 numbered squares drawn across two sheets of paper, with a button on square 60 and the word GROUND below square 1.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the track of 60 squares. Put your jumper on square 60.

setup.art: A child's hand holding six beans, with three beans being taken from a bowl labelled gravity and one bean being put into a bowl labelled air.
setup.caption: 2. Each turn, take 3 beans for gravity. Then give some back to the air.

setup.art: A button halfway down the track with a small paper parachute drawn beside it and four beans in the child's hand.
setup.caption: 3. Move down one square for each bean. Open your parachute in time to land with 4 beans or fewer.

flow.do: 1. Draw the track of 60 squares. 2. Give each player a jumper, about 15 beans and a score sheet. 3. Read the rules aloud together.
flow.say: The beans in your hand are your speed. Gravity gives you 3 beans every turn. The air takes beans back, and it takes more when you hold more.
flow.kid: Draw the track. Take a jumper and 15 beans. The beans in your hand are your speed.
flow.context: This is the first step of Open It in Time. Here you draw the track and learn the three parts of a turn.

flow.do: 1. Play one jump with the parachute closed all the way down. 2. Write the beans you hold at the end of every turn. 3. Ask what happens to the speed after turn 6.
flow.say: First we fall with the parachute closed, to see what the speed does. Write your beans after every turn. Does the speed keep growing?
flow.kid: Fall with the parachute closed. Write your beans after every turn. Does your speed keep growing?

ask.q: What happened to your speed?
good: It went 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and then stayed at 9.
It stopped growing, because the air took back as many beans as gravity gave.

flow.parent: The speeds are 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 9, 9 and 9. The jumper hits the ground on turn 9 with 9 beans. Holding 12 beans, a player gives back 3, which is exactly what gravity gave. That steady speed is the terminal speed.
flow.context: This step of Open It in Time is a jump with the parachute closed. You watch what the speed does.

flow.do: 1. Play the real game. 2. Each player chooses a turn on which to open the parachute. 3. Play to the ground and fill in the score sheet. 4. Play again and try to open later.
flow.say: Now you choose when to open. Open early and you are safe but slow. Open late and you may crash. When will you open, and why?
flow.kid: Choose when to open your parachute. Play to the ground. Did you land safely? Try again and open later.
flow.parent: Opening at the start of turn 8 is the latest safe choice. The speeds then go 6, 5 and 4, and the jumper lands on turn 10. Opening on turn 9 is too late. Let your child find this by playing.
flow.context: This is the main part of Open It in Time. Here you choose when to open the parachute and try to land safely in the fewest turns.

flow.do: 1. Ask why the speed dropped after the parachute opened, though gravity still gave 3 beans. 2. Ask what the steady speed is with the parachute open. 3. Try the heavy jumper if there is time.
flow.say: Gravity gave 3 beans every turn, open or closed. So why did your speed fall after you opened? What did the parachute change?
flow.kid: Gravity always gave 3 beans. So why did your speed drop after you opened?
flow.parent: The open parachute lets the air take back more beans at the same speed. The speed falls until the air again takes back 3 beans a turn. That happens at 3 or 4 beans. The heavy jumper must open by turn 6.

check.q: With the parachute closed, the jumper's speed stops growing at 9 beans. Why?
options: The air takes back what gravity gives
The jumper has run out of beans
check.why: Gravity gives 3 beans every turn. The air takes back more as the speed grows. When it takes back 3, the speed stops changing. A real skydiver reaches a steady speed in the same way, when air resistance equals her weight.

flow.context: This is the last step of Open It in Time. Here you explain the game with forces.

experiments.title: Table or Tub: how small a pull can start a loaded box?
experiments.context: In this experiment you pull a lunch box loaded with rice. First it stands on a table, and then it floats in a bucket. You count how much pull it takes to start the box moving each time.
experiments.question: How big a pull starts a loaded box on a table? How big a pull starts the same box when it floats on water? What happens to each pull when the load is doubled?
experiments.predict: Guess first. The box has one katori of rice in it. On the table, how many spoons of rice in the hanging bag will start it? How many with two katoris? Then guess for the floating box. Will it need more spoons, fewer spoons or about the same? Write each guess and your reason for it.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same box, the same thread and the same place on the table every time. Add the pull in equal steps: one level tablespoon of rice on the table, and one paper clip on the water. Wait 3 seconds after each step. Change one thing at a time: first the place, then the load. Do each table test 3 times and find the mean, because one run can be a fluke. Switch off the fan for the water tests, because moving air pushes a floating box.
results_table: Where the box is, and its load

materials.item: a light plastic lunch box or food box with a flat bottom, about 15 centimetres long
a bucket or tub at least 30 centimetres across, three quarters full of water (a wide tub is even better)
raw rice or dal: two full katoris for the load, and one more katori for the pull
a tablespoon
sewing thread, about 60 centimetres long
a small, light carry bag with handles, or a paper cup with a thread handle
small steel paper clips, or small safety pins
sticky tape, a ruler, a towel, a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: Wipe up spilt water at once, because a wet floor is slippery. Keep paper clips and safety pins away from children under three.

schedule.what: Pull the loaded box on the table with spoons of rice, 3 times for each load. Then float it and pull it with paper clips. Find the means and draw a chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table: spoons of rice for the two table tests, and paper clips for the two water tests. Draw the box on the table and the box on the water, with an arrow for each force. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: the pull needed to start the box, in grams
example_chart.x: Where the box is, and its load
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Here the table tests took 6 and 11 spoons of 12 grams each. Each water test took one paper clip of half a gram. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A plastic lunch box full of rice on a table, with a thread taped to its rim running over the table edge to a small hanging carry bag, and a tablespoon of rice being tipped into the bag.
setup.caption: 1. On the table, add rice to the hanging bag one spoon at a time until the box slides.

setup.art: The same lunch box of rice floating in the middle of a bucket of water, with the thread running over the rim of the bucket to one hanging paper clip.
setup.caption: 2. Float the box. Hang one paper clip on the thread and watch for 10 seconds.

setup.art: A ruler held against the side of the floating lunch box, showing how many centimetres of the box are under the water.
setup.caption: 3. Measure how deep the box sits with one katori of rice, and with two.

flow.do: 1. Put one full katori of rice in the lunch box. 2. Tape one end of the thread to the top edge of one short side of the box. 3. Put the box on the table, 30 centimetres from the edge. 4. Lead the thread over the edge and tie it to both handles of the carry bag. 5. Spread the towel on the floor under the bag.
flow.say: We are going to find the smallest pull that starts this box. The bag will pull the box, and we will add rice to the bag.
flow.kid: Put one katori of rice in the box. Tape the thread to the box. Hang the bag over the table edge.
flow.parent: The bag must hang free and not touch the table leg. Mark the place of the box with a pencil, so that it starts from the same spot every time.
flow.context: This is the first step of Table or Tub. Here you set up the loaded box on the table with a hanging bag to pull it.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the box, the tablespoon and the bucket. 2. Ask for a guess for the table with one katori, and with two. 3. Ask for a guess for the floating box. 4. Write the guesses and the reasons down.
flow.say: How many spoons will start the box on the table? What if the load is doubled? And will the floating box need more, fewer or the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess the spoons for one katori on the table. Guess for two katoris. Guess for the floating box. Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: A heavier box presses harder on the table, so there is more friction.
Water is slippery, so the box may need less pull.
The box is just as heavy on the water, so it may need the same pull.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children expect the floating box to need about half the pull.
flow.context: This step of Table or Tub is for guessing. You guess before you pull the box.

flow.do: 1. Add one level tablespoon of rice to the bag and wait 3 seconds. 2. Go on until the box slides and keeps sliding. 3. Write the number of spoons. 4. Tip the rice back and do two more runs. 5. Put the second katori of rice in the box and do 3 runs again.
flow.say: Add one spoon and wait. We want the smallest pull that starts the box. Catch the box when it slides, and put it back on its mark.
flow.kid: Add one spoon of rice to the bag. Wait 3 seconds. Stop when the box slides. Write the number. Do it 3 times for each load.
flow.parent: Expect about 4 to 9 spoons for one katori, and about twice as many for two. The numbers depend on your table and your box. If the box slides with the very first spoon, use a teaspoon instead.
flow.context: This is the table part of Table or Tub. Here you count the spoons of rice that start the box, with one katori and with two.

flow.do: 1. Switch off the fan. 2. Untie the bag and tie one paper clip to the end of the thread. 3. Float the box, with one katori of rice, in the middle of the bucket. 4. Lead the thread over the rim so that the clip hangs outside. 5. Hold the box still with one finger until the water is calm. 6. Lift your finger and watch for 10 seconds.
flow.say: Now the pull is one paper clip. That is about half a gram. Watch the gap between the box and the rim. Does it change?
flow.kid: Float the box in the bucket. Hang one paper clip on the thread. Hold the box still. Let go and watch for 10 seconds.

ask.q: What did the box do?
good: It moved slowly towards the rim.
It started very slowly and then went a little faster.

flow.parent: The box should drift towards the clip within a few seconds. If it does not, check that the thread is dry and is not stuck to a wet rim. Then add a second clip. A box that touches the side of the bucket can stick there, so start it in the middle.
flow.context: This is the water part of Table or Tub. Here one paper clip pulls the same loaded box while it floats.

flow.do: 1. With one katori in the box, let the clip pull it again and count the seconds to the rim. 2. Hold a ruler against the side of the box and read how deep it sits. 3. Put the second katori of rice in the box. 4. Test it with one paper clip, and count the seconds again. 5. Read how deep the box sits now.
flow.say: Now the load is doubled. On the table that meant about twice the spoons. What do you expect on the water? Why?
flow.kid: Count the seconds to the rim. Measure how deep the box sits. Add the second katori. Do both again.

ask.q: The box sits deeper with two katoris. What does that tell you about the upthrust?
good: The box displaces more water, so the upthrust is bigger.
The upthrust grew to match the bigger weight.

flow.parent: One clip should still start the box. It takes longer to reach the rim, because a bigger mass speeds up more slowly. The box sits deeper with two katoris. The part of the depth that comes from the rice is about twice as much as with one katori. The empty box already sat a little way into the water before any rice went in.
flow.context: This step of Table or Tub doubles the load on the floating box. You test the pull again and measure how deep the box sits.

flow.do: 1. For each table test, add the three runs and divide by 3. 2. Multiply each mean by 12 to get grams of rice. 3. Count half a gram for each paper clip. 4. Draw one bar for each of the four tests.
flow.say: A level tablespoon of rice is about 12 grams. A paper clip is about half a gram. Let's turn every result into grams and draw four bars.
flow.kid: Find the mean of the 3 runs. Multiply by 12 to get grams. Count half a gram for a clip. Draw four bars.
flow.parent: The two water bars will be too short to see beside the table bars. That is the result. Ask your child how to show it, and accept any honest way.
flow.context: This step of Table or Tub is for the means and the bar chart.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for the three sentences. 2. Ask them to draw the box on the table and on the water, with every force as an arrow. 3. Only then read the explanation together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Then draw the box twice. Which forces act on it on the table? Which on the water?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened. Draw the box twice with force arrows.

ask.q: The box is just as heavy on the water. Why did one paper clip move it there?
good: Upthrust holds the box up, so no surface grips it.
Water resistance is zero until the box moves, so nothing balances the pull.

ask.q: Why did the table pull double when the load doubled?
good: A heavier box presses harder on the table, so the friction is bigger.

flow.parent: On the table the forces are gravity, the normal force, the pull and friction. On the water they are gravity, upthrust and the pull. Water resistance appears only once the box is moving.

check.q: A loaded box floats in a bucket. Why can one paper clip start it moving?
options: The box weighs nothing in water
Water resistance is zero on a still box
The paper clip is heavier near water
check.why: Water resistance acts only on a thing that is moving through the water. A still box has none, so even a tiny pull is unbalanced. Choosing 'weighs nothing' mixes up weight and upthrust. The box weighs the same, and upthrust balances that weight.

flow.context: This is the last step of Table or Tub. Here you explain your results and draw the forces on the box.

experiments.title: The Sinking Race: which shape of dough sinks fastest?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make a ball, a pancake and a carrot from three equal pieces of atta dough. You race them in pairs through a bucket of water, to find how shape changes water resistance.
experiments.question: Three equal pieces of dough are made into a ball, a flat pancake and a carrot. Which shape sinks fastest through water, and which sinks slowest?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Put the ball, the pancake and the carrot in order, from the fastest sinker to the slowest. Write your order and your reason. Then say which of the three is heaviest, and why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Cut the three pieces from one rope of dough, all the same length, so they have the same weight. Let each shape go from just under the surface, without a push. In each race, let both shapes go at the same moment. Run each race 3 times and swap hands each time, because one hand may let go late. Change only the shape.

materials.item: half a cup of atta, about 3 tablespoons of water and a few drops of cooking oil, for a stiff dough (modelling clay also works, and sinks faster)
a bucket filled with water to about 25 centimetres deep
a ruler and a blunt knife
a phone stopwatch
a towel, a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: Do this in the bathroom or on a balcony, and wipe up spilt water. Throw the used dough away afterwards, and do not eat it.

schedule.what: Make three shapes from equal pieces of dough. Race them in pairs, 3 times each. Time the slowest shape and explain the result with forces.

experiments.record: Fill in the table of winners. Write the three shapes in order from fastest to slowest. Draw the sinking pancake with three force arrows. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: races won out of 6
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Each shape takes part in 6 races. Your numbers may be different.

setup.art: A rope of atta dough on a board, cut into three equal pieces beside a ruler, with a ball, a flat pancake and a carrot shape made from them.
setup.caption: 1. Cut three equal pieces of dough. Make a ball, a pancake and a carrot.

setup.art: Two hands holding a dough ball and a dough pancake just under the surface of a bucket of water, about a hand's width apart.
setup.caption: 2. Hold two shapes just under the water and let go of both at the same moment.

setup.art: A view down into the bucket showing the ball resting on the bottom while the pancake is still halfway down, rocking from side to side.
setup.caption: 3. Watch from above. Which shape touches the bottom first?

flow.do: 1. Knead the atta, water and oil into a stiff dough. 2. Roll a rope of dough about 2 centimetres thick. 3. Cut three pieces, each 3 centimetres long. 4. Roll one piece into a ball. 5. Press one into a flat pancake about 6 centimetres wide. 6. Roll one into a carrot about 6 centimetres long, with one thick round end.
flow.say: All three pieces come from one rope and are the same length. So they are the same amount of dough. Now we give each one a different shape.
flow.kid: Roll a rope of dough. Cut three pieces of 3 cm. Make a ball, a flat pancake and a carrot.
flow.parent: The dough must be stiff, or the pancake will droop. Press out any air pockets. If you use modelling clay, everything sinks faster, so watch closely.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Sinking Race. Here you make three shapes from three equal pieces of dough.

flow.do: 1. Lay the three shapes in a row. 2. Ask your child to put them in order from fastest sinker to slowest. 3. Ask which of the three is heaviest. 4. Write the answers and the reasons down.
flow.say: Which shape will sink fastest, and which slowest? Why do you think so? And which of the three is heaviest?
flow.kid: Put the shapes in order, fastest to slowest. Say why. Which one is heaviest?

ask.q: Which of the three is heaviest?
good: None. They are equal pieces of dough, so they weigh the same.

flow.parent: Many children say that the ball is heaviest, because it looks solid. Do not correct this yet. The question comes back at the end.
flow.context: This step of the Sinking Race is for guessing. You guess the order before any shape goes into the water.

flow.do: 1. Hold the ball just under the surface of the water. 2. Let go without pushing. 3. Watch the ball from above until it touches the bottom. 4. Lift it out and do the same with the pancake, held flat.
flow.say: This is a trial drop. Hold the shape just under the water, so that it makes no splash. Let go without a push.
flow.kid: Hold the ball just under the water. Let go. Watch it land. Try the pancake too.
flow.parent: If a shape floats, it has air in it. Knead it again and press it flat before you shape it. The pancake may rock from side to side as it sinks. That is part of the result.
flow.context: This step of the Sinking Race is a trial drop. It checks that the dough sinks and that you can see it land.

flow.do: 1. Race the ball against the pancake. Hold one in each hand, just under the surface, a hand's width apart. 2. Let go of both at the same moment. 3. A watcher says which one touches the bottom first. 4. Do the race 3 times and swap hands each time. 5. Race the ball against the carrot, thick end down, 3 times. 6. Race the carrot against the pancake 3 times.
flow.say: Let go of both at the same moment, without a push. The carrot goes thick end first. Who touched the bottom first?
flow.kid: Hold two shapes just under the water. Let go together. See which lands first. Race each pair 3 times.
flow.parent: Reshape the dough gently if it bends. If the water turns cloudy, you can still see the shapes land from above. A carrot that turns sideways is a spoilt race, so run that one again.
flow.context: This is the main part of the Sinking Race. Here you race the three shapes in pairs and write down each winner.

flow.do: 1. Time the pancake alone, from letting go to touching the bottom. 2. Do it 3 times and write each time. 3. Add the three times and divide by 3. 4. Then try to time the ball once.
flow.say: The pancake is slow enough to time. Let's get three times and a mean. Then try the ball. Can a stopwatch catch it?
flow.kid: Time the pancake 3 times. Find the mean. Then try to time the ball.
flow.parent: Expect about 2 to 3 seconds for the pancake and under 1 second for the ball. A hand on a stopwatch is off by about 0.2 seconds. So the ball's time cannot be trusted, and the races are the better test for it.
flow.context: This step of the Sinking Race times the slowest shape with a stopwatch.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for the three sentences. 2. Ask again which shape is heaviest. 3. Ask them to draw the sinking pancake with gravity, upthrust and water resistance. 4. Only then read the explanation together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Then draw the pancake. Which forces point up, and which point down?
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened. Draw the pancake with three arrows.

ask.q: The three shapes weigh the same. Which other force is the same on all three?
good: Upthrust, because each one displaces the same amount of water.

ask.q: So which force made the difference?
good: Water resistance. The pancake pushes a wide front through the water.
The carrot lets the water close up behind it.

flow.parent: Gravity points down. Upthrust and water resistance point up. Once the pancake sinks at a steady speed, the two up arrows together are as long as the down arrow.

check.q: A ball and a pancake are made from equal pieces of dough. Why does the pancake sink more slowly?
options: The pancake pushes a wider front through water
check.why: The pancake has a much bigger front area, so it meets enough water resistance at a low speed. The two pieces weigh the same and displace the same water. So gravity and upthrust are the same on both.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Sinking Race. Here you explain the order with forces and draw the forces on the pancake.

experiments.title: A Hole in the Parachute: does a vent change the fall?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make one polythene parachute that carries a coin. You drop it with no hole, then with a small hole in the top, then with a large hole. Each time you measure how long it falls and how far from a target it lands.
experiments.question: Does a hole in the top of a parachute make it fall faster? Does it change how far from the target the parachute lands?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will cut a small hole in the top of the canopy. Will the parachute then fall faster, slower or the same? Will it land nearer to the target or further away? What will a large hole do? Write each guess and your reason for it.
experiments.fair_test: Use one parachute for the whole test, so the polythene, the threads and the coin never change. Drop it from the same mark, held the same way, by the same person. Switch off the fan and close the window. Change only the hole. Do 5 drops each time and find the mean, because parachute drops vary a lot. A hand on a stopwatch is off by about 0.2 seconds, so only a bigger gap than that counts.
results_table: Distances from the X of 5 drops (cm)
Swing: a lot, a little or none

materials.item: a thin polythene carry bag with no creases, to cut one square 30 centimetres wide
sewing thread, cut into 4 pieces of 30 centimetres each
one coin, such as a 1 or 2 rupee coin
sticky tape, scissors and a ruler
paper tape or chalk, to mark an X on the floor and a line 2 metres up a wall or door frame
a phone stopwatch, a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up does the cutting and the dropping. Nobody stands on a chair or leans over a balcony. Pick up the coin after every drop.

schedule.what: Build one parachute. Drop it 5 times with no hole, 5 times with a small hole and 5 times with a large hole. Find the means and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with every time and every distance. Find the two means for each canopy. Draw a bar chart of the mean distances. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: mean distance from the X
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. In this made-up test the mean fall times were 1.9, 1.9 and 1.7 seconds. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A square of thin polythene 30 centimetres wide lying flat, with a thread taped to each corner and the four thread ends taped to one coin.
setup.caption: 1. Tape a thread to each corner of the square. Tape the four ends to one coin.

setup.art: A grown-up standing over a tape X on the floor, holding the parachute by the middle of its canopy at a tape mark 2 metres up a door frame, with the coin hanging below.
setup.caption: 2. Hold the canopy by its middle at the 2 metre mark, right above the X. Let go.

setup.art: The polythene square folded in four with a small square being cut from the folded corner, and the same canopy opened out with a small square hole in its middle.
setup.caption: 3. Fold the canopy in four and cut the folded corner to make a hole in the middle.

setup.art: A parachute lying on the floor a little way from the tape X, with a ruler measuring from the X to the coin.
setup.caption: 4. Measure from the X to the coin after every drop.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts a square of polythene 30 centimetres wide. 2. Tape one thread to each corner. 3. Hold the four loose ends together and check that the threads are equally long. 4. Tape the four ends to the coin. 5. Mark an X on the floor, and a line 2 metres up the wall above it.
flow.say: This square is the canopy. Its area is 30 times 30, which is 900 square centimetres. The coin is the load.
flow.kid: Tape a thread to each corner of the square. Tape the four ends to the coin. Mark an X on the floor.
flow.parent: A thin bag from a vegetable shop works better than a thick shopping bag. Smooth out the creases with your hand.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Hole in the Parachute. Here you build one parachute and mark the drop line and the target.

flow.do: 1. Show your child where the hole will be cut. 2. Ask for a guess about the fall time, and a reason. 3. Ask for a guess about the landing place, and a reason. 4. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: We will cut a small hole in the top, and later a large one. What will each hole do to the fall time and to the landing place? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess what a small hole will do. Guess what a large hole will do. Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think so?
good: Air will escape through the hole, so it may fall faster.
The hole is tiny beside the canopy, so it may change little.

flow.parent: Most children expect a hole to make the parachute fall much faster. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This step of A Hole in the Parachute is for guessing. You guess before any hole is cut.

flow.do: 1. The grown-up pinches the middle of the canopy and holds it at the 2 metre line, above the X. 2. The child starts the stopwatch on 'Go' and stops it when the coin lands. 3. Measure from the X to the coin. 4. Notice whether the parachute swung. 5. Do 5 drops and write every time and distance.
flow.say: These five drops are with no hole. Watch the canopy as it falls. Does it come straight down, or does it swing and slide to one side?
flow.kid: Start the stopwatch on 'Go'. Stop it when the coin lands. Measure from the X to the coin. Do 5 drops.
flow.parent: If the threads tangle or the canopy does not open, do that drop again. Expect a fall of about 1.5 to 2.5 seconds.
flow.context: This step of A Hole in the Parachute tests the canopy with no hole. You time 5 drops and measure where each one lands.

flow.do: 1. Fold the canopy in half and in half again, so its middle is at one corner. 2. Cut a square 1 centimetre by 1 centimetre off that corner. 3. Unfold it. The hole is 2 centimetres by 2 centimetres. 4. Do 5 drops, as before. Pinch the canopy just beside the hole.
flow.say: Now the canopy has a small vent. Its area is 2 times 2, which is 4 square centimetres. Watch the fall again. What is different?
flow.kid: Fold the canopy in four. A grown-up cuts a small square off the corner. Unfold it. Do 5 drops.
flow.parent: Move the threads out of the way before you fold. The hole must be in the very middle of the canopy.
