flow.context: This step of A Hole in the Parachute tests the canopy with a small hole in the top.

flow.do: 1. Fold the canopy in four again. 2. Cut the corner again, this time 5 centimetres by 5 centimetres. 3. Unfold it. The hole is now 10 centimetres by 10 centimetres. 4. Do 5 drops, as before.
flow.say: Now the hole is 10 by 10. That is 100 square centimetres out of 900. What do you expect this time? Why?
flow.kid: Fold the canopy in four. A grown-up cuts a bigger square off the corner. Unfold it. Do 5 drops.
flow.context: This step of A Hole in the Parachute tests the canopy with a large hole in the top.

flow.do: 1. For each canopy, add the 5 fall times and divide by 5. 2. Do the same for the 5 distances. 3. Draw a bar chart of the three mean distances. 4. Circle any two mean times that are less than 0.2 seconds apart.
flow.say: Let's find two means for each canopy. Times that are less than 0.2 seconds apart count as the same, because our stopwatch hand is not exact.
flow.kid: Find the mean time for each canopy. Find the mean distance. Draw three bars. Circle times that are nearly the same.
flow.context: This step of A Hole in the Parachute is for the means and the chart.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child for the three sentences. 2. Ask what the small hole cost and what it gave. 3. Ask them to draw the parachute falling steadily, with its force arrows. 4. Only then read the explanation together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Then tell me what the small hole cost us, and what it gave us.
flow.kid: Say what you thought would happen. Say what you saw. Say why it happened. Draw the falling parachute with two arrows.

ask.q: Why did the small hole change the fall time so little?
good: The hole is 4 square centimetres out of 900, so the canopy is almost as big as before.

ask.q: Where did the air go before there was a hole?
good: It spilled out under the edges, first one side and then another.

flow.parent: A small vent usually makes the fall straighter and hardly faster. With a parachute this small the difference in landing place can be slight. If your three mean distances are within 10 centimetres, say so plainly. That is your result. A large hole should shorten the fall a little.

check.q: A 2 centimetre square hole is cut in a 30 centimetre square canopy. Why does the fall time hardly change?
options: The hole removes very little of the canopy
Air cannot pass through a small hole
The hole makes the coin lighter
check.why: The canopy is 900 square centimetres and the hole is 4. So the front area is almost the same, and the air resistance balances the weight at almost the same speed. Air does pass through the hole. That is why the canopy swings less.

flow.context: This is the last step of A Hole in the Parachute. Here you explain what the hole did and draw the forces.

activities.title: Three Bottles: which one gets the biggest upthrust?
activities.context: In this activity you push three bottles of the same size under water. One is empty, one is full of water and one is full of coins and water. You find out which one the water pushes up hardest.

materials.item: three plastic bottles of the same size, with caps (about 500 millilitres each)
about 15 coins, or a handful of small stones or steel nuts
a bucket nearly full of water, in the bathroom or on a balcony
a strip of paper tape and a pencil, to mark the water level
a towel, a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Do this in the bathroom or on a balcony, and wipe up spilt water.
activities.record: Draw the three bottles under water. On each one draw an upthrust arrow and a gravity arrow. Write which arrows are the same on all three, and which are different.

setup.art: Three identical plastic bottles standing in a row: one empty with its cap on, one full of water to the brim, and one with coins at the bottom and full of water.
setup.caption: 1. Make three bottles: empty, full of water, and full of coins and water. Close all three.

setup.art: A hand pushing the empty bottle fully under the water in a bucket, with a strip of tape inside the bucket and a pencil mark at the raised water level.
setup.caption: 2. Push each bottle fully under. Mark how high the water rises.

setup.art: A bucket seen from the side with the empty bottle shooting up, the water-filled bottle hanging in the middle and the bottle of coins lying on the bottom.
setup.caption: 3. Let go of each bottle and watch what it does.

flow.do: 1. Close the first bottle with only air in it. 2. Fill the second bottle to the very top with water and close it. 3. Put the coins in the third bottle, fill it with water and close it. 4. Stick the tape upright inside the bucket, and mark the water level on it.
flow.say: These three bottles are the same size. One holds air, one holds water, and one holds coins and water. Feel how different their weights are.
flow.kid: Make three bottles: empty, full of water, and coins with water. Close them. Mark the water level in the bucket.
flow.parent: Leave no air bubble in the second and third bottles.
flow.context: This is the first step of Three Bottles. Here you make three bottles of the same size and different weights.

flow.do: 1. Hold up the three bottles. 2. Ask which one the water will push up hardest when all three are fully under. 3. Ask for the reason. 4. Write the guess down.
flow.say: Each bottle will go fully under the water. Which one will the water push up hardest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which bottle gets the biggest push up from the water. Say why.
flow.parent: Most children choose the empty bottle, because it will jump up. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This step of Three Bottles is for guessing. You guess before any bottle goes into the water.

flow.do: 1. Push the empty bottle fully under and mark the new water level. 2. Hold it just under the surface, then near the bottom, and compare the push on your hand. 3. Let go and watch. 4. Do the same with the bottle of water, and then with the bottle of coins.
flow.say: Push it right under. How far did the water rise? Is the push on your hand bigger near the bottom? Now let go. What does the bottle do?
flow.kid: Push each bottle fully under. Mark how high the water rises. Feel the push. Let go and watch.

ask.q: How far did the water rise for each bottle?
good: The same for all three, about 1 centimetre.
Each bottle displaces the same amount of water.

ask.q: What did each bottle do when you let go?
good: The empty one shot up.
The one full of water stayed almost where it was.
The one with coins sank.

flow.parent: The three marks should be at the same height. The push of the empty bottle on the hand is the same near the surface and near the bottom. The bottle of water may sink very slowly, because the plastic is a little heavier than water.
flow.context: This is the main step of Three Bottles. Here you push each bottle under, mark the water level and let go.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what the three equal marks mean. 2. Ask them to draw each bottle with an upthrust arrow and a gravity arrow. 3. Read the explanation together.
flow.say: All three bottles displaced the same water. So what can we say about the upthrust on each? Then why did they behave so differently?
flow.kid: Draw the three bottles. Give each an upthrust arrow and a gravity arrow. Which arrows are the same?
flow.parent: The upthrust arrows are equal, because upthrust depends only on the water displaced. The gravity arrows differ. The empty bottle rises because its weight is far smaller than the upthrust.

check.q: Three bottles of the same size are held fully under water. Which gets the biggest upthrust?
check.why: Upthrust equals the weight of the water displaced. Bottles of the same size displace the same water, so the upthrust is the same. The empty bottle shoots up because its weight is so small, not because its upthrust is bigger.

flow.context: This is the last step of Three Bottles. Here you draw the forces on each bottle.

activities.title: The Bag of Water: what does water weigh in water?
activities.context: In this activity you hang a bag of water from a rubber band and measure how far the band stretches. Then you lower the bag into a bucket of water and measure the band again.

materials.item: small, thin, clear plastic bags with no holes
a steel tumbler of water, about 200 millilitres
coins, all of one kind
a long, thin rubber band
thread, a ruler and a bucket nearly full of water
a towel, a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Do this in the bathroom or on a balcony. Hold the bag over the bucket, in case it leaks.
activities.record: Make a table with four rows: bag of water in air, bag of water in water, ten coins in air, and water with ten coins in water. Write the length of the rubber band for each.

setup.art: A small clear plastic bag full of water with its neck tied by thread, hanging from a stretched rubber band held in a hand, with a ruler beside the band.
setup.caption: 1. Hang a bag of water from a rubber band. Measure how long the band is.

setup.art: The same bag of water lowered fully into a bucket of water, with the rubber band above the water short and loose, and the ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Lower the bag fully into the bucket. Measure the band again.

setup.art: A second small bag holding ten coins hanging from the rubber band in air, with the ruler beside the band.
setup.caption: 3. Hang ten coins from the band in air, and measure.

flow.do: 1. Lay the rubber band on the table and measure its length. 2. Pour the tumbler of water into one bag. 3. Twist the neck to squeeze out all the air, and tie it tightly with thread. 4. Tie the rubber band to the neck. 5. Lift the bag by the band and measure the band again.
flow.say: First measure the band lying loose. Then hang the bag of water from it. How long is the band now? The stretch shows how hard the bag pulls.
flow.kid: Measure the loose band. Fill a bag with water and tie it. Hang it from the band. Measure the band.
flow.parent: If the band stretches to more than three times its length, loop two bands together. Leave no air in the bag, because an air bubble will lift it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bag of Water. Here you hang a bag of water from a rubber band in air.

flow.do: 1. Hold the bag above the bucket. 2. Ask how long the band will be when the bag is fully under water. 3. Ask for the reason. 4. Write the guess down.
flow.say: We will lower the bag into the bucket until it is fully under. How long will the band be then? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how long the band will be with the bag under water. Say why.
flow.parent: Many children expect the band to be a little shorter. Few expect it to go fully loose.
flow.context: This step of the Bag of Water is for guessing. You guess before the bag goes into the bucket.

flow.do: 1. Lower the bag slowly into the bucket, holding the band. 2. Stop when the bag is fully under and the band is above the water. 3. Measure the band. 4. Lift the bag out and watch the band stretch again.
flow.say: Lower it slowly and watch the band. What is happening? Now measure it. Compare this with the loose band on the table.
flow.kid: Lower the bag into the bucket. Watch the band. Measure it. Lift the bag out again.

ask.q: What happened to the band?
good: It went back to its loose length.
The bag pulled on it less and less, and then not at all.

flow.parent: The band should return to its loose length once the bag is fully under. The bag then hangs wherever you leave it.
flow.context: This step of the Bag of Water lowers the bag into the bucket. You measure how hard it pulls when it is under water.

flow.do: 1. Put the 10 coins in the second bag, hang it from the band in air and measure. 2. Untie the bag of water and drop the 10 coins in. 3. Squeeze out the air and tie it again. 4. Hang it from the band in air and measure. 5. Lower it fully into the bucket and measure.
flow.say: Now the bag holds water and ten coins. In air the band feels both. What will the band feel when the bag is under water? Why?
flow.kid: Hang ten coins from the band and measure. Put the coins in the water bag. Measure in air. Measure in water.
flow.parent: Under water, the band should be about as long as it was with the ten coins alone in air. It may be very slightly shorter, because the water pushes up a little on the coins too.
flow.context: This step of the Bag of Water adds ten coins to the bag. You compare its pull in water with the pull of the coins alone.

flow.do: 1. Look at the four lengths in the table. 2. Ask where the weight of the water went. 3. Read the explanation together. 4. Your child draws the bag under water with two arrows.
flow.say: The water in the bag did not get lighter. So what is holding it up? Think about the water that was in that place before the bag came.
flow.kid: Look at your four lengths. What holds the bag up in the bucket? Draw the bag with two arrows.
flow.parent: Before the bag came, the water around that place held up the water that was there. It now pushes up on the bag just as hard. So the upthrust equals the weight of the water displaced.

check.q: A bag holding 200 grams of water hangs fully under water. How hard does it pull on the rubber band?
options: As hard as it does in air
check.why: The bag displaces 200 grams of water, so the upthrust equals its weight. The two forces balance and nothing is left for the band to hold. The water in the bag still has its full weight. The water around it carries that weight.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Bag of Water. Here you work out why a bag of water pulls on nothing when it is under water.

activities.title: Newspaper on Your Chest: how fast must you walk?
activities.context: In this activity you hold a sheet of newspaper flat on your chest, let go and walk. You find the slowest speed at which the air alone keeps the sheet up. Then you fold the sheet and try again.

materials.item: one single sheet of newspaper
a clear path about 5 metres long, such as a hall, a corridor or a terrace
a notebook and a pencil

activities.safety: Clear the path first. Go in bare feet or shoes, not in socks. Keep away from stairs and from the edge of a terrace.
activities.record: Make a table with three rows: full sheet, folded in half, and folded in four. For each one write the slowest speed that kept the paper up: slow walk, fast walk, jog or run.

setup.art: A child standing still with a full sheet of newspaper held flat against the chest with both hands.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the sheet flat on your chest. Stand still and let go. It falls.

setup.art: The same child walking fast along a corridor with both arms held out to the sides and the newspaper staying flat against the chest.
setup.caption: 2. Walk and let go. Find the slowest walk that keeps the sheet up.

setup.art: The child jogging with the newspaper folded in half staying on the chest.
setup.caption: 3. Fold the sheet in half and find the new speed.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the open sheet flat against the chest. 2. They stand still and take both hands away. 3. Ask why it fell. 4. Ask whether walking could keep it up, and why.
flow.say: Hold the paper on your chest and let go. It falls. Could the air hold it there if you walked? What do you think, and why?
flow.kid: Hold the paper on your chest. Stand still and let go. Could walking keep it up? Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Newspaper on Your Chest. Here you see the sheet fall when you stand still, and guess what walking will do.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the sheet on the chest and starts to walk slowly. 2. They take both hands away while walking. 3. They try again a little faster each time. 4. They find the slowest speed that keeps the sheet up for 5 metres.
flow.say: Start slowly and let go. Did it stay? Go a little faster each time. Find the slowest speed that keeps the paper on your chest.
flow.kid: Walk and let go of the paper. Go a little faster each time. Find the slowest speed that holds it.
flow.parent: A full sheet usually stays up at an easy walk. A cotton shirt grips the paper better than a silky one. Do this indoors, because wind spoils the test.
flow.context: This step of Newspaper on Your Chest finds the slowest walking speed that keeps a full sheet up.

flow.do: 1. Fold the sheet in half. Ask what speed it will need now, and why. 2. Your child finds the slowest speed again. 3. Fold it in four and try once more.
flow.say: The folded sheet weighs the same, but it is half as wide. Will it need the same speed, a slower one or a faster one? Why?
flow.kid: Fold the paper in half. Guess the speed it needs. Test it. Fold again and test.
flow.parent: Each fold halves the front area and leaves the weight the same. So each fold needs a clearly faster speed. Folded in four, the sheet may need a run.
flow.context: This step of Newspaper on Your Chest folds the sheet and finds the new speed.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child which forces act on the sheet while it stays up. 2. Ask why the folded sheet needs more speed. 3. Read the explanation together.
flow.say: The air pushes the paper against your chest. But what stops the paper sliding down? Name every force on the paper.
flow.kid: Name the forces on the paper. Why does the folded paper need more speed?
flow.parent: Four forces act on the sheet. Gravity pulls it down. Air resistance presses it against the chest. The chest pushes back with a normal force. Friction from the shirt holds it up. A harder press from the air gives more friction.

check.q: A sheet of newspaper folded in half needs a faster walk to stay on your chest. Why?
options: Half the front area catches less air
check.why: The folded sheet has the same weight and half the front area. Air resistance grows with front area and with speed. So the smaller sheet needs more speed before the air presses it hard enough.

flow.context: This is the last step of Newspaper on Your Chest. Here you name the forces that keep the sheet up.

activities.title: Balanced or Not? Draw the forces on six things
activities.context: In this activity you draw force diagrams for six things from this unit. Some rest on a table, some float, some sink and one falls. For each one you say whether the forces are balanced.

materials.item: a notebook, a pencil and a ruler
the lunch box, the bucket and a piece of dough, to look at if you wish

activities.record: Draw six force diagrams, one for each thing. Label every arrow. Under each diagram write 'balanced' or 'unbalanced', and what the speed of the thing is doing.

setup.art: A notebook page with a simple box drawn on it and four labelled arrows: gravity down, normal force up, a pull to the right and friction to the left.
setup.caption: 1. Draw each thing as a simple box. Add one arrow for every force, and label it.

setup.art: A notebook page with six small force diagrams in two rows, each with the word balanced or unbalanced written under it.
setup.caption: 2. Under each diagram, write whether the forces are balanced.

flow.do: 1. Read the three rules aloud. 2. Draw the thing as a simple box. 3. Start each arrow on the box and point it the way the force acts. 4. Make a bigger force a longer arrow, and label every arrow.
flow.say: A force diagram has three rules. Draw the thing as a box. Draw one arrow for each force, pointing the way it acts. Make a bigger force a longer arrow.
flow.kid: Draw the thing as a box. Draw one arrow for each force. Make a bigger force a longer arrow.
flow.context: This is the first step of Balanced or Not. Here you learn the three rules of a force diagram.

flow.do: 1. Draw a loaded box on a table, pulled gently by a thread and not moving. 2. Draw the same box floating still in a bucket. 3. Ask which forces hold each box up, and which act sideways.
flow.say: First the box on the table, with a gentle pull that does not move it. Then the box floating still. Which forces act on each?
flow.kid: Draw the box on the table with a gentle pull. Then draw the box floating still. Label every arrow.

ask.q: Which forces act on the box on the table?
good: Gravity down, the normal force up, the pull one way and friction the other way.

ask.q: Which forces act on the floating box?
good: Only gravity down and upthrust up. Nothing acts sideways.

flow.parent: On the table there are four arrows in two equal pairs. On the water there are only two equal arrows.
flow.context: This step of Balanced or Not draws a still box on a table and a still box on water.

flow.do: 1. Draw the floating box at the moment a paper clip starts to pull it. 2. Draw the floating box a little later, pulled along at a steady speed. 3. Ask what is different between the two drawings.
flow.say: Now the paper clip pulls the floating box. Draw the first moment, when the box is still at rest. Then draw it moving steadily.
flow.kid: Draw the floating box when the clip first pulls. Then draw it moving at a steady speed.
flow.parent: At the first moment there is a pull and no water resistance, so the forces are unbalanced. At a steady speed, the water resistance is as long as the pull.
flow.context: This step of Balanced or Not draws a floating box as it starts to move, and once it moves steadily.

flow.do: 1. Draw a dough pancake sinking at a steady speed. 2. Draw a parachute and its coin falling at a steady speed. 3. Ask which arrows point up in each drawing.
flow.say: The pancake sinks steadily and the parachute falls steadily. Which forces point up on each one? How long must the up arrows be?
flow.kid: Draw the pancake sinking steadily. Draw the parachute falling steadily. Which arrows point up?
flow.parent: On the pancake, upthrust and water resistance point up. Together they are as long as the gravity arrow. On the parachute, air resistance alone is as long as the gravity arrow.
flow.context: This step of Balanced or Not draws a sinking pancake and a falling parachute, both at a steady speed.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the six drawings. 2. Your child writes 'balanced' or 'unbalanced' under each. 3. Ask what the speed is doing in each one. 4. Your child writes one rule that joins balance and speed.
flow.say: Look at all six. Which are balanced? In those, is the thing still, or moving at a steady speed? What rule fits them all?
flow.kid: Write balanced or unbalanced under each drawing. What is the speed doing? Write one rule.
flow.parent: Five are balanced. Only the box at the first moment of the pull is unbalanced. A good rule: when forces are balanced the speed does not change, and when they are unbalanced it changes.

check.q: A dough pancake sinks at a steady speed. Which is true of the forces on it?
options: Gravity is bigger than the upward forces
Upthrust plus water resistance equals gravity
check.why: A steady speed means the forces are balanced. Upthrust and water resistance point up, and together they equal gravity. If gravity were still bigger, the pancake would keep speeding up.

flow.context: This is the last step of Balanced or Not. Here you sort the six drawings and find the rule.

activities.title: Parachute or Rocket? Plan a landing on four worlds
activities.context: In this activity you read a table about the air and gravity of four worlds. For each world you decide how a spacecraft should slow down to land: with parachutes, with rocket engines, or with both.

materials.item: the table of four worlds on this card
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Make a table with four rows: Earth, the Moon, Mars and Titan. For each world write your landing plan and your reason. Then write what real spacecraft did there.

setup.art: Four small worlds in a row labelled Earth, Moon, Mars and Titan, with a thick haze round Earth and Titan, a very thin haze round Mars and none round the Moon.
setup.caption: 1. Read how thick the air is on each world.

setup.art: A notebook table with four rows and a child's drawing of a parachute, a rocket flame or both beside each world's name.
setup.caption: 2. Choose a parachute, a rocket or both for each world, and say why.

flow.do: 1. Read the table together. 2. Ask what a parachute needs in order to work. 3. Ask which world will be hardest for a parachute.
flow.say: A parachute works by pushing on air. Look at the air on each world. Where will a parachute work well? Where will it not work at all?
flow.kid: Read the table. What does a parachute need? Which world is hardest for a parachute?

chart.title: Air and gravity on four worlds, compared with Earth
rows: About one hundredth as thick as Earth's
About four times as thick as Earth's
chart.note: Thick here means how much air there is in each litre.

flow.context: This is the first step of Parachute or Rocket. Here you read how thick the air is on four worlds.

flow.do: 1. For each world, your child chooses parachutes, rocket engines or both. 2. They write a reason that uses the air and the gravity. 3. Ask which world needs the biggest parachute for the same load.
flow.say: Choose a plan for each world, and give a reason from the table. Where would you need the biggest parachute? Where would the smallest one do?
flow.kid: Choose a parachute, a rocket or both for each world. Write your reason.

ask.q: Why can no parachute work on the Moon?
good: The Moon has no air, so there is no air resistance.

ask.q: Why is Titan the easiest world for a parachute?
good: The air is thick and the gravity is weak, so a small canopy balances the weight at a low speed.

flow.context: This step of Parachute or Rocket is for planning. You choose how to land on each world.

flow.do: 1. Read what real spacecraft did. 2. Your child compares each one with their plan. 3. Ask why the Mars rover needed both a parachute and rockets.
flow.say: On the Moon, Chandrayaan-3 landed in 2023 with rocket engines alone. On Mars, a rover landed in 2021 with a parachute and then rockets. On Titan, a probe landed in 2005 under parachutes alone.
flow.kid: Read what the real spacecraft did. Was your plan the same? Why did Mars need both?
flow.parent: Chandrayaan-3 landed on the Moon on 23 August 2023. The rover Perseverance landed on Mars on 18 February 2021, with a parachute 21.5 metres wide and then rockets. The probe Huygens landed on Titan on 14 January 2005, after about two and a half hours under parachutes. Capsules that bring people back to Earth use parachutes for almost all of the slowing.

check.q: Why did the Mars rover need rockets as well as a very large parachute?
check.why: The air on Mars is about one hundredth as thick as the air on Earth. Even a very large parachute cannot slow a heavy rover enough in such thin air. Rockets do the last part of the slowing.

flow.context: This is the last step of Parachute or Rocket. Here you compare your plans with real landings.

activities.title: Watch a Bird Land: how does a pigeon use air resistance?
activities.context: In this activity you watch pigeons or crows from a window as they land. You note what each bird does with her wings, tail and body in the last second before she touches down.

materials.item: a window or balcony from which you can see birds land
a notebook and a pencil

activities.record: Make a tally table with four rows: wings spread wide, tail fanned out, body tilted up, legs stretched forward. Add a tally mark each time you see a landing bird do that thing.

setup.art: A child at a window with a notebook, watching a pigeon about to land on a ledge.
setup.caption: 1. Watch birds landing on a ledge, a wire or the ground.

setup.art: A pigeon just before landing, with her wings spread wide, her tail fanned out, her body tilted up and her legs stretched forward.
setup.caption: 2. Tally what she does with her wings, tail, body and legs.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child how a flying bird slows down to land. 2. Ask what she might do with her wings and tail. 3. Draw the tally table.
flow.say: A pigeon has no brakes on a wheel. How does she slow down before she lands? What do you expect her to do with her wings and tail?
flow.kid: How does a flying bird slow down to land? Guess what her wings and tail do.
flow.context: This is the first step of Watch a Bird Land. Here you guess how a bird slows down.

flow.do: 1. Watch for birds coming in to land. 2. For each landing, look at the wings, the tail, the body and the legs. 3. Add tally marks. 4. Try to see at least 3 landings.
flow.say: Watch the last second before she touches down. Are her wings narrow or wide? Is her tail closed or fanned? Which way is her body tilted?
flow.kid: Watch 3 landings. Look at the wings, tail, body and legs. Add tally marks.
flow.parent: If no bird lands in six minutes, try again in the early morning or evening. Pigeons and crows land most often near food and on ledges.
flow.context: This is the main step of Watch a Bird Land. Here you tally what landing birds do.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what the bird did to her front area. 2. Ask what that did to the air resistance. 3. Compare her landing with a parachute.
flow.say: She spread her wings and tail and tilted up. What did that do to the area she pushed through the air? So what happened to the air resistance?
flow.kid: What did she do to her front area? What did that do to the air resistance?
flow.parent: A landing bird makes her front area as big as she can. The air resistance grows and slows her in a short distance. In fast flight she does the opposite, and keeps her body narrow and smooth.

check.q: A pigeon fans her tail and spreads her wings just before she lands. What does this do?
options: Her front area and air resistance grow
check.why: Spread wings and a fanned tail push a much bigger area through the air. Air resistance grows with front area, so she slows down quickly. Her weight does not change.

flow.context: This is the last step of Watch a Bird Land. Here you explain the landing with air resistance.

projects.title: The Parachute Trial: design, test and improve a parachute in three days
projects.context: In this three-day project you design a parachute that carries two coins. It must fall slowly from 2 metres and land close to a target. You test a standard design first, then change one thing at a time, and write a report.

materials.item: thin polythene carry bags
sewing thread
coins, all of one kind
a sheet of newspaper and an old cotton handkerchief, as other canopy materials
sticky tape, scissors and a ruler
paper tape or chalk for an X on the floor and a line 2 metres up a wall
a phone stopwatch, a notebook and a pencil

projects.safety: A grown-up does the cutting and the dropping. Nobody stands on a chair or leans over a balcony.

schedule.what: Build the standard parachute and drop it 5 times. Find its mean fall time and its mean distance from the X. Choose two things to change.
Test your two changes, one at a time, with 5 drops each.
Build your final design, test it with 5 drops and write a one-page report.

projects.record: Write a one-page report. It has a labelled drawing of your final parachute and a table of the two means for every design. It has a force diagram of the steady fall. It ends with one sentence on what you would change next.

setup.art: A square polythene parachute 30 centimetres wide with four threads taped to two coins, lying beside a ruler and a notebook.
setup.caption: 1. Build the standard parachute: a 30 centimetre square, four threads of 30 centimetres, two coins.

setup.art: Three parachutes side by side: a larger square one, one with eight sides and eight threads, and one with a small hole in the top.
setup.caption: 2. Change one thing at a time: the size, the shape, a vent, the threads or the material.

setup.art: A notebook page with a labelled drawing of a parachute, a table of means and a force diagram with two equal arrows.
setup.caption: 3. Test the final design 5 times and write the report.

flow.do: 1. Build the standard parachute: a polythene square 30 centimetres wide, four threads of 30 centimetres, and two coins taped together. 2. A grown-up drops it 5 times from the 2 metre line above the X. 3. Write each fall time and each distance from the X, and find the two means. 4. Your child chooses two things to change, and says what each should do.
flow.say: The task is to carry two coins down slowly and land near the X. First we need numbers for the standard design. Then choose two things to change, and tell me why.
flow.kid: Build the standard parachute. Drop it 5 times. Find the mean time and the mean distance. Choose two things to change.
flow.parent: Things to change: the size of the canopy, its shape, a vent, the length of the threads, the number of threads or the material. To make eight sides, cut the four corners off the square and use eight threads.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Parachute Trial. Here you build and measure the standard parachute, and choose what to change.

flow.do: 1. Build a parachute with the first change only. 2. Drop it 5 times and find the two means. 3. Build another with the second change only, and do the same. 4. Compare each with the standard design.
flow.say: Change only one thing in each parachute. Then we know what caused any difference. Which change helped the fall time? Which helped the landing?
flow.kid: Make one change. Drop it 5 times. Then test the second change by itself. Compare with the standard design.

ask.q: Why do we change only one thing at a time?
good: If two things change together, we cannot tell which one made the difference.

flow.parent: A mean time less than 0.2 seconds from the standard counts as no change. Newspaper is heavier and stiffer than polythene, and usually falls faster.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Parachute Trial. Here you test two changes, one at a time.

flow.do: 1. Your child decides the final design from the results. 2. Build it and drop it 5 times. 3. Count how many drops land within 30 centimetres of the X. 4. Your child writes the one-page report.
flow.say: Use your results to choose the final design. Does it fall slowly? Do at least 4 drops out of 5 land within 30 centimetres of the X?
flow.kid: Choose your final design. Drop it 5 times. Count the drops that land near the X. Write your report.

check.q: A new parachute has a bigger canopy and longer threads, and it falls more slowly. What can you say?
options: You cannot tell which change caused it
check.why: Two things were changed together, so either one could have slowed the fall, or both. A fair test changes one thing at a time. Then any difference has only one possible cause.

flow.context: This is day 3 of the Parachute Trial. Here you build and test the final design and write the report.

challenges.title: The Slow Sinker: make a piece of dough sink as slowly as you can
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. In the Sinking Race, a flat pancake of dough sank far more slowly than a ball of the same dough. Here you shape one piece of dough so that it takes as long as possible to sink.
challenges.problem: Take one piece of stiff atta dough, cut 3 centimetres long from a rope 2 centimetres thick. Shape it so that it takes as long as possible to sink 25 centimetres in a bucket of water.
constraints: Use only the one piece of dough, and add nothing to it.
The shape must sink by itself. A shape that floats or holds an air bubble does not count.
Let the shape go from just under the surface, without a push.
Time each shape 3 times and use the mean.
materials: stiff atta dough or modelling clay
a bucket filled with water to about 25 centimetres deep
a ruler and a blunt knife
a towel, a notebook and a pencil
general: Press the dough into a pancake that is as wide and thin as it can be without tearing.
Roll the dough into a long, thin noodle and let it go lying level.
creative: Give a small pancake long, thin arms, like a star. Many tiny living beings of the sea, called plankton, have long spines that slow their sinking.
Make a thin ribbon and give it one twist, so that it turns as it sinks.
Make a shallow saucer and let it go open side up, with no air under it.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own slow sinker. Draw it, make it and time it 3 times. What was the mean? Which helped more: a bigger front area, or a shape that stirs up more water?

setup.art: A piece of dough cut from a rope beside a ruler, and next to it a flat dough pancake about 6 centimetres wide.
setup.caption: 1. Start with one piece of dough. Time a 6 centimetre pancake first, as the time to beat.

setup.art: A star-shaped piece of flat dough with long thin arms sinking slowly through a bucket of water, with a phone stopwatch held above.
setup.caption: 2. Make a new shape, let it go just under the surface and time it.

flow.do: 1. Press the piece of dough into a pancake 6 centimetres wide, as in the Sinking Race. 2. Let it go flat, from just under the surface. 3. Time it 3 times and find the mean. 4. Write this as the time to beat.
flow.say: First we need the time to beat. In the Sinking Race, the pancake was the slowest shape. How long does it take to sink?
flow.kid: Make a pancake 6 cm wide. Time it 3 times. Find the mean. This is the time to beat.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Slow Sinker. Here you time a 6 centimetre pancake of dough, as the time to beat.

flow.do: 1. Read the usual ideas: a wider pancake, a long noodle, a ring. 2. Your child chooses one and says why it should be slower. 3. Make it, time it 3 times and find the mean.
flow.say: Which idea do you think will sink most slowly? Why? Let's test your choice 3 times.
flow.kid: Pick one idea. Say why it should be slower. Make it. Time it 3 times.

ask.q: Why should a wider, thinner pancake sink more slowly?
good: It has a bigger front area, so it meets enough water resistance at a lower speed.

flow.parent: Very thin dough folds up as it sinks, and then it falls faster. Finding the limit is part of the challenge.
flow.context: This step of the Slow Sinker tests one of the usual ideas.

flow.do: 1. Your child designs a shape of their own and draws it. 2. They make it and time it 3 times. 3. They compare the mean with the time to beat. 4. They change one thing and test again.
flow.say: Now design your own slow sinker. What will you change, and why? Did it beat the pancake?
flow.kid: Design your own shape. Draw it. Make it. Time it 3 times. Change one thing and test again.
flow.parent: Once a shape sinks steadily, the water resistance on it equals its weight minus its upthrust. That is the same for every shape made from this piece. A slower shape meets that resistance at a lower speed.

check.q: Many plankton have long, thin spines. How do the spines help them stay in sunlit water?
options: The spines add water resistance and slow sinking
check.why: Spines give a tiny body a much bigger area for the water to push against. The plankton then sink very slowly, so they stay longer near the surface, where there is light.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Slow Sinker. Here you design, test and improve your own shape.

challenges.title: The Quiet Dive: enter the water with the smallest splash
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about meeting water at speed. You drop pieces of dough from 30 centimetres into a bowl of water. You shape the dough so that it makes the smallest splash.
challenges.problem: Drop one piece of dough from 30 centimetres above a bowl of water. Shape the dough so that the water splashes the shortest distance out of the bowl.
constraints: Use one piece of dough each time, cut 3 centimetres long from a rope 2 centimetres thick.
Hold the dough 30 centimetres above the water and let go. Do not throw it.
After each drop, measure from the rim of the bowl to the farthest wet spot on the newspaper.
Drop each shape 3 times and use the mean.
materials: stiff atta dough or modelling clay
a wide steel bowl or vessel, nearly full of water
four or five sheets of dry newspaper to spread under the bowl
general: Make the dough narrow, so that it meets less water at once.
Roll a short rod and drop it end first.
Smooth the surface of the dough with a wet finger.
creative: Shape a long cone and drop it point first. A kingfisher's beak is a long, narrow wedge, and she dives into water with hardly a splash.
Make a long shape with a point at both ends, so that the water can close up gently behind it.
Eiji Nakatsu, an engineer in Japan who watched birds, shaped the nose of a fast train like a kingfisher's beak. The train then entered tunnels more quietly.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own quiet diver. Draw it, make it and drop it 3 times. What was the mean splash distance? What does your shape have in common with a kingfisher's beak?

setup.art: A wide steel bowl nearly full of water standing on spread sheets of dry newspaper, with a hand holding a flat dough pancake one ruler's length above the water.
setup.caption: 1. Stand the bowl on dry newspaper. Hold the dough 30 centimetres above the water and let go.

setup.art: Dark wet spots on the newspaper around the bowl, with a ruler measuring from the rim of the bowl to the farthest spot.
setup.caption: 2. Measure from the rim to the farthest wet spot.

setup.art: A long dough cone falling point first towards the water, beside a small drawing of a kingfisher diving beak first.
setup.caption: 3. Shape the dough so that it makes the smallest splash.

flow.do: 1. Stand the bowl on dry newspaper. 2. Drop a flat pancake of dough, held level, from 30 centimetres. 3. Circle the wet spots with a pencil and measure to the farthest one. 4. Do the same with a ball of dough. 5. Change the newspaper when it gets too wet.
flow.say: First we need a splash to beat. Drop the pancake flat, and then the ball. Which one throws water further? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Drop a flat pancake into the bowl. Measure to the farthest wet spot. Then drop a ball.
flow.parent: The pancake usually makes the widest splash, because it meets a lot of water at the same moment.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Quiet Dive. Here you measure the splash of a flat pancake and of a ball.

flow.do: 1. Read the usual ideas: a narrow shape, a rod dropped end first, a smooth surface. 2. Your child chooses one and says why it should splash less. 3. Make it, drop it 3 times and find the mean distance.
flow.say: Which idea should make the smallest splash? Why? Let's test your choice 3 times.
flow.kid: Pick one idea. Say why it should splash less. Make it. Drop it 3 times.

ask.q: Why should a narrow shape splash less?
good: It has a small front area, so it pushes less water aside at once.

flow.context: This step of the Quiet Dive tests one of the usual ideas.

flow.do: 1. Your child designs a shape of their own and draws it. 2. They make it and drop it 3 times. 3. They compare the mean with the pancake and the ball. 4. They change one thing and test again.
flow.say: Now design your own quiet diver. What will you change, and why? Did the splash get smaller?
flow.kid: Design your own shape. Draw it. Drop it 3 times. Change one thing and test again.
flow.parent: A long cone dropped point first usually makes the smallest splash. If it tips over in the air, hold it upright by the thick end and let go cleanly.

check.q: A long cone dropped point first makes a smaller splash than a flat pancake. Why?
options: The cone moves water aside little by little
check.why: The point meets a tiny patch of water first, and the cone widens slowly. So the water is moved aside gently. The flat pancake has to move a wide patch of water all at once, and that water is thrown outward.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Quiet Dive. Here you design, test and improve your own shape.

worksheets.title: Four forces and how they act (core)

items.p: Which force from water acts on a boat that is not moving?
items.why: Upthrust pushes up on anything in water, still or moving. Water resistance acts only on a thing that moves through the water.

items.p: True or false: water resistance acts on a floating box that is perfectly still.
items.why: False. Water resistance comes from pushing water out of the way, so a still box has none. A strong answer adds that upthrust does act on the still box.

items.p: Air resistance and water resistance together are called ____.
items.why: Drag is the force from any fluid against a thing moving through it. Air resistance is drag in air, and water resistance is drag in water.

items.p: Sort these forces: can each one act on a still thing, or only on a moving thing?
items.why: Friction can hold a still thing in place. Upthrust and gravity act all the time. Air resistance and water resistance act only on a thing that moves through the air or water.
cats: Can act on a still thing
Acts only on a moving thing
items: Can act on a still thing
Acts only on a moving thing
Can act on a still thing
Acts only on a moving thing
Can act on a still thing

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.why: These words are used all through the unit. A strong answer could give an example of each.
pairs: Upthrust
the upward push of water or air on a thing in it
Streamlined
rounded in front and narrowing slowly behind
Terminal speed
the steady speed a falling thing reaches
Displace
to push water aside and take its place
Vent
a small hole in the top of a parachute

items.p: Draw a box floating still in a bucket. Add an arrow for each force on it, and label the arrows.
items.a: A box on a water line with two arrows of the same length: gravity pointing down and upthrust pointing up.
items.why: A strong drawing has only two arrows, and they are equal, because the box is still. An arrow pointing sideways shows a mix-up, because nothing pushes a still floating box sideways.
items.art: A bucket of water with a plain box floating on the surface and no arrows.

items.p: On a table, a loaded box needs 6 spoons of pull to start. With double the load, about how many?
items.why: A box that is twice as heavy presses twice as hard on the table. So the friction is about twice as big. 6 × 2 = 12.

items.p: Put the steps of a fair parachute test in order.
a: Build one parachute and mark the drop line
Guess what the hole will do, and say why
Drop it 5 times before and after cutting the hole

items.p: True or false: a stone lying on the bed of a pond gets no upthrust.
items.why: False. The stone displaces water, so the water pushes up on it. The upthrust is smaller than the stone's weight, so the stone stays down.

items.p: In Three Bottles, an empty bottle and a bottle of coins got the same upthrust. Explain why.
items.a: The two bottles are the same size, so they displace the same amount of water. Upthrust equals the weight of the water displaced. So it is the same for both.
items.why: A strong answer says that upthrust depends on the water displaced, not on the weight of the thing. It may add that the empty bottle rises because its weight is so small.

items.p: When the forces on a thing are balanced, its speed does not ____.
items.why: Balanced forces cancel. A still thing stays still, and a moving thing keeps the same speed.

items.p: Three of these make drag bigger. Which one makes it smaller?
items.why: More speed, a wider front and a thicker fluid all make drag bigger. A streamlined shape lets the fluid close up smoothly behind, so the drag is smaller.

items.p: On a drawing of a parachute, label the canopy, the vent, the threads and the load.
a: Vent: the small hole in the top
Threads: the lines from the canopy to the load
items.why: A strong answer can also say what each part does. The canopy gives a large front area, and the vent lets a little air out through the middle.
items.art: A round parachute with a small hole in the top, lines running down and a small box hanging below, with four blank label lines.

items.p: A ball and a pancake of equal dough sink in water. Which one sinks more slowly?
items.why: The pancake has a much bigger front area, so it meets more water resistance at the same speed. The two weigh the same, so 'the heavier one' cannot be right.

items.p: A swimmer wears a tight cap and keeps her body straight. Say how each one lowers water resistance.
items.a: The cap makes her head smooth, so water flows past it easily. A straight body has a small front area and lets the water close up behind her.
items.why: A strong answer names front area or shape for the straight body, and smoothness for the cap.

worksheets.title: Balanced forces, upthrust and fair tests (stretch)

items.p: A skydiver falls at a steady 200 kilometres an hour. How big is the air resistance on her?
items.why: A steady speed means balanced forces. Air resistance points up and gravity points down, so the two are equal. Choosing 'smaller' usually means thinking that a falling thing must have a bigger force downward.

items.p: In the Bag of Water, the rubber band went loose when the bag was under water. Explain why.
items.a: The bag displaced its own weight of water. So the upthrust on the bag equalled its weight, and nothing was left for the band to hold.
items.why: A strong answer says that the water around the bag pushes up on it. That push is as big as the weight of the water displaced. It does not say that the water in the bag became lighter.

items.p: True or false: at twice the speed, drag is about twice as big.
items.why: False. At twice the speed, drag is about four times as big. That is why going fast costs so much energy.

items.p: Five parachute drops land 20, 35, 10, 25 and 30 centimetres from the X. What is the mean, in centimetres?
items.why: 20 + 35 + 10 + 25 + 30 = 120. Then 120 ÷ 5 = 24. The mean distance is 24 centimetres.

items.p: One paper clip pulls a loaded floating box. The box starts very slowly. What makes the start slow?
opts: Water resistance on the still box
The mass of the loaded box
items.why: A still box has no water resistance, and water has no friction to hold it. The box starts slowly because a big mass takes time to speed up under a small pull.

items.p: Draw a dough ball sinking at a steady speed. Show three forces with arrows of the right lengths.
items.a: A ball with gravity pointing down, and upthrust and water resistance pointing up. The two up arrows together are as long as the down arrow.
items.why: A strong drawing makes the upward arrows add up to the downward one, because the speed is steady. A gravity arrow that is longer than both together would mean the ball is still speeding up.
items.art: A plain ball in the middle of a tank of water with no arrows.

items.p: Three people talk about the hole in the top of a parachute.
items.a: A strong answer uses the fall times and landing distances from A Hole in the Parachute. It chooses one view and gives a fair point from another. For example, the child is right that a very large hole speeds up the fall.
items.why: Each view holds part of the truth. A hole does let air out. A small hole costs very little speed. And how much it costs depends on its size, which only a test can show.

views.who: A child seeing a parachute for the first time
views.says: A hole lets the air out. The parachute will fall faster, and the jumper will be hurt.
A small hole steadies the fall and costs almost no speed. I always cut one.
It depends on the size of the hole. I would measure three sizes before I decided.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Use your results from A Hole in the Parachute as evidence. Then say what one of the others has right.

items.p: Put these shapes in order of drag, from least to most. They have the same front area and speed.
items.why: The fish shape lets the fluid close up smoothly behind it. The ball leaves a wake, and the flat plate leaves the widest wake of all.

items.p: The upthrust on a thing equals the weight of the water it ____.
items.why: This is Archimedes' principle. The water around a thing pushes up as hard as it pushed on the water that was there before.

items.p: Match each place to the way a spacecraft can slow down to land there.
items.why: A parachute needs air to push against. No air means rockets only. Very thin air means a parachute and rockets. Thick air means parachutes can do the work.
pairs: The Moon, with no air
rocket engines only
Mars, with very thin air
a parachute and then rockets
Titan, with thick air
parachutes alone
Deep space, far from any world
nothing slows it, so it keeps its speed

items.p: Two mean fall times, timed by hand, are 1.9 and 2.0 seconds. What can you say?
opts: The gap is too small to trust
items.why: A hand on a stopwatch is off by about 0.2 seconds. A gap of 0.1 seconds is smaller than that, so the two parachutes may be the same.

items.p: Three of these get an upthrust. Which one does not?
items.why: A boat and a stone are in water, and a balloon is in air, so each displaces a fluid. The Moon has no air or water, so nothing pushes up on the hammer.
opts: A stone on a pond bed
A hammer falling on the Moon

items.p: On a drawing of a fish, label the rounded front, the widest part and the narrowing tail.
a: Widest part: about one third of the way back
Narrowing tail: the long back half of the body
items.why: A strong answer adds that the long, narrowing tail lets the water close up smoothly, so the wake is small.
items.art: A side view of a rohu fish with three blank label lines.

items.p: A full newspaper sheet stays on your chest at a walk. Folded in four, it needs a run. Why?
items.a: The folded sheet has the same weight and a quarter of the front area. So the air must push much harder on each part of it. That needs a higher speed.
items.why: A strong answer says that the weight is unchanged, the front area is smaller, and air resistance grows with speed.

items.p: True or false: a parachute falling at a steady speed has more air resistance than weight.
items.why: False. At a steady speed the two are equal. If air resistance stayed bigger than the weight, the parachute would slow to a stop and then rise.

items.p: One paper clip moved a heavy floating box in Table or Tub. Is a heavy thing always hard to move? Explain.
items.a: On the table, the heavier box needed a bigger pull, because friction grew with the weight. Afloat, one paper clip moved the box with either load. So the weight was not what held the box. Friction was.
items.why: A strong answer uses both parts of the test, and names friction as the cause on the table. It may add that a big mass still makes the start slow.

items.p: Two people argue about whether air resistance is a kind of friction.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives two pieces of evidence. For the book: both act against movement and make heat. For the engineer: drag is zero at rest, grows with speed and does not grow with weight. It also grants the other side a point.
items.why: This is a real disagreement about a name. The facts are agreed. What differs is which likeness each person thinks matters most.

views.says: Air resistance is friction with the air. It acts against movement and makes heat, as friction does.
Drag is different. It is zero on a still boat, and it grows with speed, not with weight.

items.ask: Pick a side. Give two pieces of evidence from this unit. Then say what the other side has right.

items.p: A boat's engine pushes with 300 newtons, and the boat keeps a steady speed. How big is the water resistance?
items.why: A steady speed means balanced forces, so the resistance equals the push. Choosing 'less than 300' usually means thinking that a moving thing needs a bigger force forward.

items.p: A steel ball and a table tennis ball of equal size fall from a tower. Which lands first? Why?
items.a: The steel ball lands first. At the same speed both meet the same air resistance, because they have the same size and shape. That resistance soon balances the light ball's weight. The steel ball must go much faster before its weight is balanced.
items.why: A strong answer says that air resistance depends on size, shape and speed, not on weight. It then compares that resistance with each ball's weight.

items.p: True or false: pushing a closed bottle deeper under water makes the upthrust on it bigger.
items.why: False. Once the bottle is fully under, it displaces the same water at any depth. The water presses harder on its top and on its underside by the same amount.

items.p: A canopy is 30 centimetres by 30 centimetres. A hole is 10 by 10. How many square centimetres are left?
items.why: 30 × 30 = 900 and 10 × 10 = 100. Then 900 − 100 = 800 square centimetres.

items.p: A cyclist doubles her speed. About how many times as big is the air resistance now?
items.why: At twice the speed, drag is about four times as big. She meets twice as much air each second, and she hits it twice as fast.

items.p: A space capsule gets hot mainly because it ____ the air in front of it.
items.why: The capsule squashes the air in front of it very hard and very fast, and squashed air gets hot. Rubbing along the sides adds only a little heat.

items.p: Sort each change: does it make a parachute's steady fall slower, or faster?
items.why: A bigger canopy or a lighter load balances at a lower speed. A heavier load, a very large hole or thinner air needs a higher speed before air resistance equals the weight.

items.p: Draw a parachute in the first second after it opens, while it is still slowing. Show both forces.
items.a: A parachute with gravity pointing down and air resistance pointing up. The air resistance arrow is the longer one.
items.why: A strong drawing makes the upward arrow longer, because the parachute is slowing down. Equal arrows would mean a steady speed.
items.art: A plain open parachute with a small load and no arrows.

items.p: A coin is dropped into deep water. Put what happens in order.
a: Gravity is bigger than upthrust, so the coin speeds up
Water resistance grows as the coin gets faster
The upward forces become equal to gravity
The coin sinks at a steady speed
items.why: Resistance grows with speed until the forces balance. After that the speed stays the same.
items: The upward forces become equal to gravity
The coin sinks at a steady speed
Gravity is bigger than upthrust, so the coin speeds up
Water resistance grows as the coin gets faster

items.p: A fish and a dolphin are not close relatives, yet they have nearly the same shape. Suggest why.
items.a: Both move fast through water, and water resistance is the same for any body. Over many generations, the animals with shapes of lower drag caught more food and escaped more often. So both ended up with a streamlined shape.
items.why: A strong answer joins the shape to water resistance, and says that the same water acts on both animals.

items.p: Match each thing to the reason it stays where it is.
items.why: Only a solid grip or a rope can hold a thing against a sideways push. In water, upthrust can hold a thing up, but it cannot stop the thing drifting.
pairs: A boat tied to a jetty
the rope pulls against wind and current
A book on a tilted desk
friction matches the pull down the slope
A fish hanging in a pond
upthrust equals her weight
A coin on a pond bed
the normal force and upthrust equal its weight

items.p: Three of these are still uncertain. Which one is settled?
items.why: Archimedes' principle has been tested for more than two thousand years. Turbulence and the skins of dolphins and sharks are still being studied.
opts: How much a dolphin's skin lowers drag
That upthrust equals the weight displaced
How much shark skin lowers drag

items.p: Design a test: do longer threads make a parachute fall more slowly? Say what you keep the same.
items.a: Make two parachutes that differ only in thread length, such as 15 and 45 centimetres. Keep the canopy, the load, the drop height and the person the same. Drop each 5 times and compare the mean times.
items.why: A strong answer changes only the thread length, repeats each drop and compares means. It may add that a gap under 0.2 seconds is too small to trust.

quiz.p: Which of these forces always points up?
quiz.why: Upthrust is the upward push of water or air. The other three point against a movement or a slide, whichever way that is.

quiz.p: A loaded box floats still in a tub. How much water resistance acts on it?
quiz.why: Water resistance acts only on a thing that moves through the water. Upthrust is the force that equals the weight of the box.

quiz.p: On a table, what happens to the pull needed to start a box when its load is doubled?
quiz.why: Friction grows with the weight pressing the surfaces together. Twice the load gives about twice the friction to overcome.

quiz.p: Which change makes the air resistance on a cyclist smaller?
quiz.why: Bending low makes the front area smaller. Riding faster, sitting upright and loose clothes all make air resistance bigger.

quiz.p: Which shape has the least drag in water at the same speed and front area?
quiz.why: The fish shape is rounded in front and narrows behind, so water closes up smoothly and the wake is small.

quiz.p: What does the upthrust on a thing under water depend on?
opts: How much water the thing displaces
What the thing is made of
quiz.why: Upthrust equals the weight of the water displaced. Choosing 'how heavy' usually comes from seeing light things rise. They rise because their weight is smaller than the upthrust.

quiz.p: A bottle weighs less than the water it displaces. What does it do when let go under water?
quiz.why: The upthrust equals the weight of the water displaced, which is more than the bottle's weight. The forces are unbalanced upward, so the bottle rises.

quiz.p: A coin sinks at a steady speed. What is true of the forces on it?
quiz.why: A steady speed means balanced forces. Upthrust and water resistance together equal gravity.

quiz.p: Three parachute designs land, on average, 30, 31 and 29 centimetres from the target. Single drops of one design vary by 20 centimetres. What can you say?
opts: The designs are too close to tell apart
quiz.why: The means differ by only 2 centimetres, and single drops vary by ten times that. So the test cannot tell these designs apart.

quiz.p: What does a small vent in the top of a parachute mainly do?
opts: Lets air out, so the canopy swings less
quiz.why: Air caught under the canopy leaves through the vent and not under the edges. The canopy swings less, and the fall is hardly faster.

quiz.p: The same parachute carries a heavier load. What happens to its steady falling speed?
quiz.why: A heavier load needs more air resistance to balance it. The same canopy gives more air resistance only at a higher speed.

quiz.p: Which of these can nobody yet work out exactly?
quiz.why: The equations for turbulent flow have never been solved exactly. The other three are settled.

applications: Parachutes are used for people, for supplies dropped from aeroplanes and for space capsules. The canopy is sized to suit the load, and it has a vent.
Ship designers pull model hulls along long tanks of water to measure their water resistance before a ship is built.
Racing cyclists bend low and wear smooth clothes and long-tailed helmets. Fast trains such as the Vande Bharat have a sloping nose.
Cargo ships often sail more slowly than they could. A small cut in speed gives a large cut in water resistance and in fuel.
Ships and boats are held by ropes and anchors, and moved in harbour by tugs. Water alone cannot hold a ship in place.
Submarines take in water to sink and push it out to rise. A life jacket adds a lot of size and little weight, so it adds upthrust.
Heat shields protect space capsules from the white-hot air squashed in front of them.

open_questions.q: Can the equations for moving air and water always be solved?
open_questions.why_open: They were written about two hundred years ago. For swirling, turbulent flow nobody has found exact answers, or proved that exact answers always exist.

open_questions.q: Exactly when and why does smooth flow break into swirls?
open_questions.why_open: Osborne Reynolds studied this in pipes in 1883. Scientists can now predict it for a simple pipe, but not for most real shapes.

open_questions.q: How much do the skins of dolphins and sharks lower water resistance?
open_questions.why_open: Some tests of surfaces copied from shark skin show small savings, and others show none. Living skin is hard to test at swimming speed.

open_questions.q: Do fish in a school save energy by swimming in each other's wakes?
open_questions.why_open: Some measurements find a saving and some do not. It depends on where each fish swims, and that is hard to follow in a large school.

open_questions.q: Can a heavy crewed spacecraft be landed on Mars?
open_questions.why_open: The air on Mars is too thin for parachutes alone and thick enough to cause great heating. Engineers are still testing ways to slow a heavy craft there.

maths.problem: In Table or Tub, three runs on the table took 5, 7 and 6 spoons of rice. What is the mean? How many grams is that, at 12 grams a spoon?
maths.answer: The mean is 6 spoons, which is 72 grams.
maths.explain: Add the three runs: 5 + 7 + 6 = 18. Divide by the number of runs: 18 ÷ 3 = 6 spoons. Each spoon is about 12 grams, so 6 × 12 = 72 grams.
maths.context: This is about Table or Tub. A hanging bag of rice pulls a loaded lunch box on a table. You count the spoons of rice that start it.

chart.title: Made-up example: three runs on the table

maths.why_maths: One run can be a fluke. The mean of three runs is a number you can trust more. Grams let you compare it with the paper clip.

maths.problem: On the table, a loaded box needed a pull of 72 grams to start. Afloat, it needed one paper clip of half a gram. How many times as big was the pull on the table?
maths.explain: Divide the bigger pull by the smaller one. 72 ÷ 0.5 is the same as 72 × 2, which is 144. So the pull needed on the table was 144 times as big as the pull needed on the water.
maths.context: This is about Table or Tub. The same loaded lunch box is pulled on a table and then while it floats in a bucket.
maths.why_maths: The two bars are so different that one cannot be seen beside the other. Dividing tells you how many times bigger one is.

maths.problem: A parachute canopy is a square 30 centimetres wide. A small vent is a square 2 centimetres wide, and a large one is 10 centimetres wide. What fraction of the canopy does each hole remove?
maths.answer: The small hole removes 1 part in 225. The large hole removes 1 part in 9.
maths.explain: The canopy is 30 × 30 = 900 square centimetres. The small hole is 2 × 2 = 4, and 4 out of 900 is 1 out of 225. The large hole is 10 × 10 = 100, and 100 out of 900 is 1 out of 9. So the small hole changes the front area very little.
maths.context: This is about A Hole in the Parachute. You cut a small square hole, and then a large one, in the top of a polythene canopy.
maths.why_maths: Air resistance depends on area. Working out the areas shows why a small vent hardly changes the fall time.

maths.problem: Air resistance is about 4 times as big when the speed doubles. A cyclist meets 10 newtons at 15 kilometres an hour. About how much does she meet at 30, and at 60?
maths.answer: About 40 newtons at 30 kilometres an hour, and about 160 newtons at 60.
maths.explain: From 15 to 30 the speed doubles, so the resistance is 10 × 4 = 40 newtons. From 30 to 60 it doubles again, so 40 × 4 = 160 newtons. Four times the speed gives sixteen times the resistance.
maths.context: This is about Newspaper on Your Chest. There you found that the air pushes harder when you move faster. This problem uses the rule that scientists have measured.
maths.why_maths: A rule lets you predict speeds you cannot test at home. It also shows why going fast costs so much energy.

maths.problem: The graph shows a jumper's speed in Open It in Time. On which turn did the speed stop growing? On which turn did the parachute open? What was the landing speed?
maths.answer: The speed stopped growing on turn 6, at 9 beans. The parachute opened on turn 8. The landing speed was 4 beans.
maths.explain: The line climbs to 9 on turn 6 and stays level on turn 7. So 9 is the terminal speed with the parachute closed. On turn 8 the line drops from 9 to 6, so the parachute opened then. The last point, on turn 10, is at 4 beans.
maths.context: This is about the game Open It in Time. The beans in your hand are your speed. Gravity gives 3 beans a turn, and the air takes some back.

chart.title: Speed of a jumper in Open It in Time

maths.why_maths: A line graph shows at a glance where a speed grows, where it is steady and where it changes suddenly.

maths.problem: A box 20 centimetres long and 10 centimetres wide floats with a load. Box and load together have a mass of 540 grams. One cubic centimetre of water has a mass of 1 gram. How deep does the box sit?
maths.explain: A floating box displaces its own mass of water, so it displaces 540 cubic centimetres. The base of the box is 20 × 10 = 200 square centimetres. Depth is volume divided by base area: 540 ÷ 200 = 2.7 centimetres.
maths.context: This is about Table or Tub. There you measured how deep a loaded lunch box sat in the water. You did it with one katori of rice and with two.
maths.why_maths: Upthrust equals the weight of the water displaced. With volume and area you can predict how deep a boat will sit before you load it.

maths.problem: A skydiver falls 3,300 metres at 55 metres each second with her parachute closed. Then she falls 1,100 metres at 5.5 metres each second with it open. How long does each part take, and how long is the whole jump?
maths.answer: 60 seconds, then 200 seconds. The whole jump takes 260 seconds, which is 4 minutes and 20 seconds.
maths.explain: Time is distance divided by speed. 3,300 ÷ 55 = 60 seconds. 1,100 ÷ 5.5 = 200 seconds. Together that is 260 seconds. 240 seconds make 4 minutes, and 20 seconds are left over. The short last part takes most of the time. A speed of 55 metres each second is about 200 kilometres an hour.
maths.context: This is about the game Open It in Time. There the jumper fell fast with the parachute closed and slowly with it open. This problem uses round numbers for a real skydiver.
maths.why_maths: Dividing distance by speed shows how much longer a parachute keeps a jumper in the air. It also shows why she must open it in good time.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that a parachute needs a hole in the top? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: On 22 October 1797, André-Jacques Garnerin rose over Paris under a hydrogen balloon. About 900 metres up by most accounts, he cut the rope that held him to it. He came down in a basket under a parachute of light cloth about 7 metres wide. It was the first parachute jump from a balloon high in the air. The canopy had no hole. It seemed plain that a parachute should hold all the air it caught. The parachute did slow his fall, but it swung wildly from side to side all the way down. Garnerin landed unhurt and badly shaken. The astronomer Jérôme Lalande is said to have seen what was wrong. Air trapped under the canopy has to get out. It was spilling out under one edge and then under the other, and tipping the canopy each time. He is said to have suggested cutting a hole in the top, so that the air could leave through the middle. Parachutes made with this hole swung far less, and fell hardly any faster. On 12 October 1799, Garnerin's pupil Jeanne-Geneviève Labrosse is credited as the first woman to jump by parachute. Almost every round parachute since then has had a vent at the top.
how_we_found_out.who: André-Jacques Garnerin, who made the jump. Jérôme Lalande, who suggested the vent. Jeanne-Geneviève Labrosse, the first woman to jump by parachute.
how_we_found_out.when: 22 October 1797 (Garnerin's jump over Paris) and 12 October 1799 (Labrosse's jump)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a parachute canopy should have no opening, so that it holds all the air it catches. A canopy with a vent at the top swings far less and falls almost as slowly.
how_we_found_out.art: A man in a small basket under a ribbed pale parachute swinging far to one side above the roofs of Paris, with a small balloon drifting away above.

roots.context: We have learned how friction, air resistance, water resistance and upthrust differ, and how they act together. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In Table or Tub, the loaded box on the table stayed still until several spoons of rice pulled it. Afloat, the same box moved for one paper clip, even with double the load. Friction can grow to match a pull, but water resistance begins only when a thing moves. So water can slow a floating thing, but water alone can never hold it in place.
deep_truth.habit: We say a heavy thing is hard to move because it is heavy. On land the real cause is friction, which grows with the weight. Take the friction away, and the smallest pull moves the heaviest load, only slowly.
deep_truth.evidence: In Table or Tub, two katoris of rice needed about twice as many spoons as one katori on the table. Afloat, one paper clip started both loads. The heavier load only took longer to get going.

three.who_am_i: You live at the bottom of an ocean of air. The air pushes up on you a little all the time, and pushes back whenever you run.
three.what_is_life: Every swimmer and every flyer has a body shaped by the water or air they move through. A fish, a dolphin and a penguin have nearly the same outline, because they move through the same water.
three.what_is_this_world: The same water holds a boat up and slows the boat down. The holding up comes from the weight of the water. The slowing comes from the boat's own movement.

roots.thread: Friction, air resistance, water resistance and upthrust have four names. Underneath, they are one kind of event. The particles of one thing come very close to the particles of another, and electric forces act between them. Upthrust is the push of water particles that are squeezed by the water above them. Resistance is the push of particles that have to be moved out of the way. Friction is the grip between the particles of two solid surfaces. One kind of force between particles shows up as holding up, slowing down or gripping. Which of these we see depends on what the things are doing.

teachings.teaching: Nothing in the world is softer or weaker than water. Yet nothing is better at wearing down what is hard and strong.
teachings.link: Water gives way to the smallest slow push. One paper clip moved the loaded box in Table or Tub. Yet the same water pushes back hard on anything that moves fast.

teachings.teaching: An old man swims safely in a wild river. He says that he goes under with the swirls and comes out with them. He follows the way of the water and does not force his own way.
teachings.link: Water resists a swimmer only as much as she moves through it. A swimmer carried along with a current meets almost no resistance from that current.

science.text: The upthrust on a thing equals the weight of the fluid it displaces (Archimedes, about 250 BCE).
A thing keeps the speed it has unless the forces on it are unbalanced (Newton's first law, 1687).
Nobody can yet work out exactly how swirling water or air will move.

other_view.view: The loaded box did resist the paper clip, with its mass. A heavier floating thing takes longer to speed up and longer to stop. So the old belief is half right. Weight does not hold a floating thing in place, but mass still makes it slow to change.

practice.title: Let the water carry your arm
practice.say: Sit beside a bucket of water. Lower one hand and wrist into the water and let them go loose. Feel the water take some of the weight of your hand. Now move your hand very slowly from side to side. Feel how little the water pushes back. Now move it fast, three times. Feel the water push hard. Hold your hand still again. The push is gone, and the water is still carrying you.
practice.kid: Put one hand in a bucket of water. Let it go loose. Feel the water carry it. Move it very slowly. Now move it fast. Hold it still again.

ask: The same water holds the box up and slows the box down. Is that one push or two?
Water resistance is there only while a thing moves. So is the force in the water, or in the moving?
Water cannot hold a floating thing in place. What holds you in place when you stand still?

playtest: The experiments and activities in this unit were reasoned through step by step. They have not yet been tried at home. Please treat the amounts as a starting point. Table or Tub (core) needs a light plastic lunch box, raw rice, thread, a bucket and a few paper clips. The number of spoons depends on your table and your box. Expect about 4 to 9 spoons for one katori and about twice as many for two. One paper clip should start the floating box within a few seconds. If it does not, dry the thread and the rim. Start the box in the middle of the bucket and switch off the fan. The Sinking Race (core) uses stiff atta dough. Dough with air in it floats, so knead it well. The ball and the carrot sink in under a second, so they are raced side by side and not timed. Only the pancake is slow enough for a stopwatch. A Hole in the Parachute (core) needs a grown-up to cut and to drop. Small polythene parachutes vary a lot from drop to drop. A small vent usually steadies the fall. With a canopy this small, the difference in landing place can be slight. The unit asks the child to report honestly if the means are too close to tell apart. Three Bottles and the Bag of Water wet the floor, so do them in the bathroom. In the Bag of Water, squeeze every bubble of air out of the bag, or it will float. Newspaper on Your Chest needs about 5 metres of clear floor and still air. The Quiet Dive wets several sheets of newspaper. Watch a Bird Land depends on a bird arriving, so you may need a second try at dawn or dusk. No part needs a garden. Facts checked on 17 Nov 2026 against NASA/JPL, ESA, ISRO, Crossref and the Clay Mathematics Institute: the Garnerin and Labrosse dates, the Perseverance, Huygens and Chandrayaan-3 dates, the Perseverance parachute width, the 2000 prize, the journal citations and the museum and PhET links.
